286921.body:
Hi, this has no doubt been asked and answered before, but I haven't found the answer yet...

How many intersections/corners are there for each harbor?  I'm playing the new 4th edition.  It looks like the harbor streches along a single hex side, which would mean that there are TWO possible corers where I could build a harbor settlement, or does the harbor fill the entire triangular inlet, so that there are THREE possible corners to build a harbor settlement (this would mean that two players could share the harbor), or is it just the innermost corner, where the two hexes join so that there os just ONE possible harbor settlement?  

The illustrations in the manual are confusing on this point, as the habors appear to cover one whole hex side (implying two adjoining corners to settle), but all of the harbor illustrations show the settlement at the "inner" corner, implying only ONE possible harbor settlement.

I hope that that makes sense.

Thanks heaps,
Lee Borkman

Each harbor has two possible building locations, so only one player could build on a single harbor.  Some of the game editions show an outline of a 1/4 circle in the corners to indicate where the building can be placed.  

The following image is the best picture that I have found that demonstrates the two locations, although it may not exactly match the harbor pieces in your 4th edition..

Thanks very much, guys.  That picture of the older edition tile makes it very clear.  A choice of TWO possible points to settle per harbor.

Thanks again for your help,
LBB

487502.body:
We are currently playing a three-person game and over what seems like a rather trivial issue a deep rift has occurred in which my boys are refusing to play any more. 

Please Help!!!!

So, if someone plays the Monopoly development card are they allowed to ask beforehand (i.e. before anyone knows they're going to play it...) whether anyone has a particular item? (in this instance it was sheep, so, having ascertained that my other son had sheep my eldest was able to get all three off him with this card. It felt like, at best, trickery and at worst cheating. 

So, veteran Cataners - which (if any) is it? 

Thanks for the help - we can't carry on til we get an answer so a quick and definitive reply will be GREATLY appreciated...
I have not seen it mentioned in the rules but I would consider it unfair.

Legal. And common.

S.




And very, very evil.  Better make sure you can win the game right then.  Otherwise, you'll be facing an embargo the rest of the game.

The target player has the right to lie if the player is just fishing for information. (Part of the game is trying to keep track of what the other players have.) The key to using the Monopoly card is listening to failed trades and then exploiting that information, which is perfectly acceptable.

Of course, it really depends on how old the boys in question are!

Yes, quite legal.  If you are watching the rolls closely then you should know more-or-less what everyone has so you should not have to ask.

However, you are not even asking about the most NASTY use of Monopoly.  This is when you do a 'generous' trade with someone - e.g. give them 2 ore for a sheep and THEN monopoly the ore back into your hand.  People get really upset at that, but it is also within the rules.
It's sharp play but not illegal.

All of your responses are MUCH appreciated...

My eldest who started the skullduggery is 17 and my youngest, the recipient and HUGELY scandalised player is 13... 

At the moment they're playing again after the compromise of only taking 2 of the 3 sheep from him, which just about seems to have calmed things down... 

My eldest, when told I was coming on here said: "hang on, do those gamers have morals?" worried was he that your integrity would affect his chances... 

You've just GOTTA love gaming haven't you????? :laugh:

OF COURSE NOT!

137897.body: Just putting the finishing touches to the translation of the Big Box rules (which means that my girlfriend is proofreading it). I mentioned on the thread dealing with that (http://www.boardgamegeek.com/article/1200987) the idea of doing a complete annotated rule set for Carcassonne including, well, whatever we think is necessary. The Big Box rules are a good basis for doing this, since they bring RGG and HiG rules a little more into line than they were before, and include a couple of changes which make all the expansions more compatible than before (builders and pigs are not followers any more - they can't be move to the city of Carcassonne, or put on top of towers). For an overview of the changes see this post: http://www.boardgamegeek.com/article/1200987#1200987. And, because of the more standardised rules, a number of the FAQ from my site (http://carcassonnefaq.blogspot.com) are obviously out-of date. So it seems like a good time to go through everything an try to create a standard

Simply put, if you're using the RGG rules which came with the original release of the games, you aren't using the newest RGG rules.

The English Big Box set does contain consolidated rules rather than just a compilation of the old rules. I started a thread dealing with this here: http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/133953.
The table below summarises the various sets:
http://homepage.mac.com/mjharper/summary.jpg
A '?' means I don't yet know what the RGG Big Box rules have to say about the issue. The problem is however, that RGG have changed some rules, such as builders and pigs not being followers anymore (as in the HiG Big Box), corrected others, such as meeples on towers being allowed to be captured (as they always were in HiG rules), and left some unchanged, such as 1st edition farmer scoring and small cities. The whole aim of the complete annotated rules is to comprehensively describe the most current set of rules and highlight the differences between sets…

I'm an avid gamer who likes to buy games my daughter can play with me (she is 6). Seeing as how many others had reported playing Carcassonne with their 6 year olds (and younger), I decided to give it a try. After a few turns, she picked up all the mechanics and played a very solid game. I helped her win some good points, and I made some mistakes myself (it WAS my first time, after all). In the end, I ended up winning by 1 point. We left out the farmer scoring (as was recommended).

I won't say I'm suprised by the strategies that became apparent as the game got longer (strategies I wasn't aware of at first), because many others have pointed out how deep the game can be. But I saw a number of places where good strategic play could have been used to great effect.

I especially liked when she drew a cloister, and found a space for a tile that was already surrounded by farms. She put the tile down and scored 9 points on that one play! She definitely liked that.

Overall, I thought it was GR

:star: If you are averagely lucky, she will be happy to play the occasional game with you and your kid(s) as they grow up. Thank your stars that she is this willing to participate in your hobby.
:star: If you are unlucky she will never want to play the games again. Start or join a game group.

Some people are gamers, some definitely aren't. You stand a good chance of bringing up a gamer but you will never change your wife if she falls into the latter camp, so no point causing friction. Just enjoy sharing the things you enjoy sharing and enjoy gaming as a hobby you do apart from her.

Good post Michael.Welcome to BGG. 

I'll add this to the list of games to play with the kids when they're older (Daniel is 18 mo. and our daughter is due in Feb).

Well done. Sounds promising. Take it slow but keep at it, you might have another convert there.

On another note, I managed to get my mother-in-law to play with me and my daughter. She and I spent the majority of our time trying to win control of a city, while my daughter kept completing things. I guess I should just learn when to give up on a city, because in the end, my daughter helped grandma and cut me off from the city completely, costing me a huge investment in points. Needless to say, grandma and granddaughter both beat me. I still have some strategy to learn...

Perhaps best of all, grandma LOVED the game. That actually suprised me, because she usually (like my wife) does not play games. She talked about it 3 more times that evening, after the game was over. In my opinion, if you are still thinking about the game hours later, you like the game. I'll definitely have to give her another chance at it!

The Liverpool shipyard site is the only one that can be built in the canal period. All three, Liverpool included, can be built during the rail period.

You can upgrade another player's coal or iron industry only if there are no cubes available on the map AND the corresponding coal or iron demand track is empty.

But wouldn't building over another player's industry deny that player victory points for their completed industry? :what:

(editted for clarity)

You will only be able to build a shipyard in Liverpool in the Canal Period.

Should be one of the following:

* You will be able to only build a shipyard in Liverpool in the Canal Period.
=> During the Canal Period, you cannot flip a shipyard built in Liverpool.


OR

* You will be able to build only a shipyard in Liverpool in the Canal Period.
=> During the Canal Period, nothing can be built in Liverpool except a shipyard.

OR

* You will be able to build a shipyard only in Liverpool in the Canal Period.
=> During the Canal Period, Liverpool is the only place you can build a shipyard.

OR

* You will be able to build a shipyard in Liverpool only in the Canal Period.
=> You cannot build a shipyard in Liverpool during the Rail Period.


The moral of the story is to keep your modifiers close to their verbs and nouns.

Yes, this is true.  I tried to cover that in the following exception:

2. External ports printed on map allow access to distant and external markets, as do flipped or un-flipped port tiles.

But obviously there's still a little bit of ambiguity.

I would not include this in the first post, but here's a more verbose answer:


Shipping Cotton

Choose one of your unflipped cotton mills.  Do one of the following:

1. Choose an unflipped port that is connected to your cotton mill.  Flip both tiles.

2. *If* your mill is connected to any kind of port and the distant market isn't bottomed out, you may sell to the distant market.  Flip a demand tile and lower the demand.  If it bottoms out, your action ends and your mill does not flip.  If demand remains, then flip your mill and gain additional income equal to the remaining demand.

You may repeat the above choice for as many mills as you have.  However, if you choose the distant market and the demand bottoms out, your action must immediately end.

That exception sounds pretty firm to me.  

I brought that up because when i was playing outside my group (there was one player in particular who has played many times, too) and i shipped through an unflipped port to a distant market he crinkled up his forehead and questioned if i could do that. I agree with the re-write also as the original made it look like you had to match each unflipped Cotton Mill with its own unflipped Port (ie. in pairs) in order to sell multiple batches of cotton cloth. As long as you are connected to any "constructed port" (ie. flipped or unflipped Port or any off-board location) you can (almost) flip any number of Cotton Mills as you wish. The "almost" comes in when you have no further unflipped Ports on the board (or you choose not to flip them) and you are now dealing with the distant market lottery.

The clever trick is to concisely capture all this in one or two lines...

A number of people have commented that while the connection and card rules may be thematic, they're too complicated and too confusing.  While Brass is a tricky game to teach, explaining these rules in-theme makes them actually comprehensible.  Here's my approach:

0. Contrary to popular belief, Lancashire does actually have a very nice road network. But carting large, heavy lots of goods on them isn't a profitable way to do business*, so it turns out only iron cubes can move on the roads.

1. Coal is needed in such huge quantities that it you can't do business without a connected coal source. And it's so heavy that you have to use the nearest available source, because the porter's guild insists on it.

2. Cotton is fluffier than coal, but is still a bulky good moved in high volumes, and thus, needs to be connected to a port for shipment. However, it's a much higher-value item, so the porter's guild will take it to any port, not just the closest one.

Here is a list of changes and rebalances we are introducing in our version of Brass: Lancashire.

Changes to the components:

level 1 cotton mills changed from 3 to 5 points

After analyzing data from orderofthehammer.com that building lvl 1 cotton mills is strongly correlated with losing. We have thus increased the points moderately. We still feel that a player should almost never play a level 1 cotton mill as the return is so poor, but now believe that there are at least edge cases where it is now a viable play.

2 cards removed from the deck (one coal and one cotton)

To make setting up the rail phase simpler, and to reduce some edge cases where players can be unwittingly helped or hindered by the random cards that were removed.

Virtual link between Birkenhead and Liverpool removed

597032.body: Can someone explain the green science cards to me? I know 7 Wonders is an easy game, but for some reason I just can't understand how to score these cards. Every time we play, we have to consult the book and/or the one guy in our gaming group who understands the rules.

There are 3 symbols.
A. Make as many complete sets of the 3 different symbols as you are able and multiply by 7.

B.Then look at each individual symbol. Count how many you have of each individual symbol. Square each number. Add these to the total from A.

That's how many points you have.

And yes, you'll be using some cards twice. Once in the complete sets and once in the single sets.

I'm not sure how the following symbol plays out.

"Once this symbol enters play, you can construct the first age card in each color for free" 

There are 7 cards per age and 7 different colors, so does this mean you could potentially play all 7 cards (assuming they're difference colors) for free for a whole age?

"Age card" is the name of the cards (to differentiate them from "Leader cards" or from other types of card); but that may lead to obscure phrasing.

What that symbol does is unrelated to the various ages.
If you have 0 red (military) cards in your empire, the first red card you build is free.
If you have 0 green (scientific) cards in your empire, the first green card you build is free.
If you have 0 purple (guild) cards in your empire, the first purple card you build is free.
If you have 0 white (leader) cards in your empire, you still have to pay for the first one, because Leaders are not "age cards".
And so on, and so forth.

Once you've built the first one in one color, the symbol does nothing for future cards of that color, not even in subsequent ages.

Ah thanks! That appears to make more sense. So it refers to the cards in your empire and not the cards in your hand. I guess you could potentially play all cards for free in a age but they would have to be the first of each color in your empire.

Exactly.
Also note that grey (manufactured goods) cards already cost nothing, and that by the time you unlock Olympia's step II you'd probably already have at least one brown (raw material) card; so the number of "free cards" you'll actually get from that symbol won't be so high.

… consists of carrying out exactly two actions, one per die. Once a die has been used, it is placed onto the used die storage space in the upper right hand corner of the player’s board.

(ellipsis points theirs)

and a sidebar next to that

Starting with the start player and then continuing in turn order, each player uses their dice to carry out two actions

In a nutshell, I read the instructions in the car on the way home from Gen Con. We didn't play it for the first time until a few days later.

I assumed players would play one of their dice in turn and then play another like so many other games I'd played (assumed straight forward).  Our references back to the rule book were focused on learning the icons and benefits of the buildings and knowledge tiles.  Who would think I'd need to verify how many dice we got to play???  Oops.

I've played it both ways (made the same mistake at first).  It definitely strengthens the Ship action if people take two actions at once.  Being last in a four player game can feel pretty brutal - just watch all those beautiful tiles snapped up before you have a chance to get them, especially with the dearth of tiles left towards the end of a year.

But winning in last all game is certainly possible - just need to take tiles early in the year, have a plan to use non-tile taking actions in the later half of the year and to stock up on workers for added flexibility at the end of a year to be prepared for the next one.

We've played a few games with the rule change and more than anything at this point we seem to be looking for and taking more combinations more than anything else.  I believe we still have some things to learn yet.

1- The FP uses a character/WotW die to move the fellowship; the fellowship progress counter is moved forward 1 space.

2- The SP rolls a number of dice equal to the number of RED action dice in the hunt box, to a max of 5.

3- Normally, each roll of a 6 is a success. If the fellowship moved this turn before, there will be BLUE action dice in the hunt box. For each BLUE die, add 1 to the result of each die roll. - A stronghold controlled by the SP
- At least 1 Nazgul

1060625.body:
This came up a couple of times while explaining the game at the PD-Verlag booth during the SPIEL fair in Essen.

What happens when you play the Diplomat card to copy the Prefect card of another player who happens to also have the Praefectus Magnus card? Do you activate the Praefectus Magnus and double the production bonus?

- The Praefectus Magnus is not activated in this case. You cannot copy the Praefectus Magnus, only the Prefect card is copied.


What happens when you play the Diplomat card to copy the Prefect card of another player while having the Praefectus Magnus card yourself? Do you activate the Praefectus Magnus and double the production bonus?

- The Praefectus Magnus is activated in this case, because you have it and you use a Prefect (via the Diplomat) to let a province produce goods (not money).
This strikes me as being an obvious application of the rules as written and also the only way to not make Diplomat super-broken. I'm glad you clarified it for us.

The currently available rules cover this case (emphasis added):If a player who currently owns the PRÆFECTUS M. plays a Prefect card (or uses one with the Diplomat) in order to let a province produce, he receives a double bonus (2 units instead of 1). Production inside the cities is not affected.
This makes explicit the second item in the OP.

One could argue that the explicit statement here also implies (by omission) the first item of the OP.

1060638.body:
If you were able to get one of the first copies of the game you may encounter one of the following errors:

Action of the Colonist card (second part): The rulebook says to take two Sestertii for every colonist you have on the board (as an alternative to building new colonists), the card itself says to take five Sestertii plus one for every colonist you have on the board. - The card is correct. The rulebook has a slightly older version of the rule, which was modified last-minute to make the Colonist more useful early in the game, when you do not have that many colonists on the board.

Cost of the Diplomat card in subset number IV (English card set only): The card states "Food" as cost (in the red area at the bottom) but shows the symbol for tools (the anvil). - The symbol is correct, the cost of the card is tools, not food.

1320853.body:
The Architect card says "Move Your Colonists Then Build in Cities Adjacent To Your Colonists."


Is the "Move" required?  Can a player choose to

A) NOT MOVE ANYWHERE and simply build in cities adjacent to where her colonists are currently placed?

B) MOVE ONE COLONIST at least one space away and then build adjacent to where any of his colonists are (even the ones not moved, OR

C) NO CITIES CAN BE BUILT WHERE A COLONIST HAS NOT FIRST BEEN MOVED?

Montebanc

You are not required to move. However, if you want to move you must move before building, not after.

You can build adjacent to any of your colonists, regardless of what you did with your movement.

Jon Ben is perfectly right: 
You don't have to move, it's only an option! 
(the rulebook should clarify this)
Enjoy!
Mac
If a colonist is located inside a city (it's initial placement from colonize) can I then build in adjacent cities or do i have to move the colonist to a line first?
A colonist in a city is not adjacent to any other city.

Thus in your specific example, then yes you would have to move a colonist.

If the question is general, then no you don't have to move any colonists from playing the architect card.  They may already be in position from a previous architect card, but you did not have enough resources and/or money the previous time.

3336157.body:
Most people I play with do not understand Mercator's trade rule (trade up to 2 types of goods.) They try to sell 2 goods and buy 2 goods. Last night for instance, no matter how much I described it, they didn't get it.

"You can sell 2 types of goods."
"You can sell 1 type of good and buy 1 type of good."
"You can buy 2 types of goods."
"And that's it."

For people who teach a lot and have not had trouble with people understanding it, how do you teach that?

Perhaps I can give them a visual reference.

You can do 2 transactions.

A transaction is selling any number of a type of good, or buying any number of a type of good.

If they're truly somehow not getting it by explanation, then I would simply show them a couple of examples! E.g. buy 3 wines and sell 2 bricks.
Yeah, that's nice, thank you. Any other ideas?

Yeah, that's nice, thank you. Any other ideas?

Show the common mistake. “here, I’m selling three cloth, that’s one transaction, even though it’s three items as they are all the same type of good. Now I want to buy tools and food but I cannot do both as I only have one transaction left. I can buy any number of food that I can afford, or any number of tools, but cannot have both types.”

Perhaps try to make them choose the two types of "authorized" goods for their action first, then then can buy/sell whatever quantity they want, in any order.
(the idea being to clearly separate the constraint on the types from the rest of the trading action, which is "do whatever you want" once the limit on types is understood)

It is a tricky rule, definitely something where I go "pay attention, this next rule is something that someone will get wrong later.". This phrasing often works with my players as they then want to prove me wrong.

Something that I haven't tried but that might help some players that rely on physical signifiers: you could give a new player five of the leftover city markers from the unused letter. When using the merkator, they must first pick two of those markers, buying or selling only in those types they've selected.
I say something like you can interact with (or exchange or transact) two types of goods, whether buying or selling. You can buy or sell as many units of those two goods as you'd like/are able to.

Similar to the previous response I usually say, "You receive 3 money and then you can buy or sell goods of up to two different types. You can buy or sell as much as you like but you can only ever touch two different types of good."

I tell them...  You can visit 2 stores...  The brick store and the cloth store or the wine store and the food store.  Whichever two stores you decide to visit, those are the only types of goods you can buy or sell this turn.

I tell them...  You can visit 2 stores...  The brick store and the cloth store or the wine store and the food store.  Whichever two stores you decide to visit, those are the only types of goods you can buy or sell this turn.
That's the one I think I'm going to stick with. We used that last night and it seemed to work. Thank you.

You can do 2 transactions.

A transaction is selling any number of a type of good, or buying any number of a type of good.

If they're truly somehow not getting it by explanation, then I would simply show them a couple of examples! E.g. buy 3 wines and sell 2 bricks.
Yup Transaction would be the only way to describe it if they didn't get it from you can buy 2 or sell 2 or a combination of the above.

I enumerate examples. "You can sell any number of one type of good and buy any number of a different good. You sell two types. You can buy two types. You don't have to do everything: you could buy just one type, or sell just one type. You could even mercator for money and buy/sell nothing. What you can't do is buy/sell more than two types: you can't sell one type and buy two types."

Intro to these “overviews before rules” I do:
The goal is to make reading rules easier, for those who want to spend the time. Sounds weird? I'll try to explain...
I love a variety of games but I find there’s an issue with rulebooks. A catch 22 if you will.
Rulebooks (and rule teaches) must be exact, but that creates a lot of time a feeling of anxiety for people as they start reading and wondering “When will it all tie together for me?”, “when will I say ‘ok, THAT’S the game!’?”. Some rulebooks aren’t read or understood because of that, and it’s a shame as many times the game is simpler than was considered.
To prevent that anxiety you need an overview which tells the story of the game (be it in written or video format). You tell a story differently than the way someone explains exact rules. The problem is that rulebooks cannot contain such an overview as it will make them too long, or feel like you’re reading rules twice – hence the catch. But some people do want to spend a few minutes
Seems like too much detail to me, almost the full rules.

Sometimes a good overview isn't about abridging the rules, especially if there aren't a whole lot of them. Sometimes it's about rearranging them.. at least that's how I found Concordia to be.

But the test is one and one only - Do people, who do not know the game (and possibly tried to understand it but didn't), are more prone to understanding it after reading it. If you already know the rules, you don't need this overview.

Looking at this one as typical of both, there's an awful lot in the overview that should rightly be in the teach only. (And not in both.)

I enjoy teaching in person and typically give an overview in advance of getting into the details. Whilst I ad lib to some extent I do prepare the structure in written form and review it in advance, sometimes casually referring to it whilst teaching. For some games I've written out the overview that I say (a version of) before teaching the rules.

Concordia happens to be one of those games:
The Roman civilization existed from the mid 8th century BCE to the late 5th century CE - around 1300 years. Concordia is set in an historical approximation of the empire's height circa 100CE - a time of great prosperity & relative peace. At least if you were a Roman!

Players are Roman merchants establishing trading houses in the provinces, reap

Spirit Island has a dedicated online, mobile-friendly living FAQ. It's specifically geared for "I'm in the middle of this game and have a question...". All FAQ entries are tagged, and you can do simple text searches (no ANDs or ORs, though you can search on partial words). The back of the Spirit Island rulebook has both a (shortened) hyperlink and QR Code to the FAQ site, so you shouldn't need to find this forum post to look stuff up.

The engine it's running on (Querki) is in beta, so there may occasionally be bugs - for instance, at the moment of this posting there's some trouble adding links from FAQ entries back to the discussion threads which spawned them - but actual downtime is rare and generally short.

The FAQ entries are written and edited by me and a couple of awesome & knowledgable volunteers from among the long-time playtesters / >G. (Thank you!!!) If you have a question that the rulebook doesn't answer (or which it does answer, but still seems ambiguous to you), and you d

Jagged Earth has resulted in many thorny rules questions. After much work, discussion, and thought, I've just posted FAQs for a whole bunch of them - done as a batch partly because some affect each other, partly so I could post a summary page.

So here it is: A whole bunch of FAQs, updates, clarifications, and a few reversals of previous rulings! It has a TL;DR overview at the top and more explanation beneath (with links to actual FAQ entries).

- - - -

There's one errata that's important enough that I'll mention it here, though:

Errata: During Setup only, add exactly 1 additional Blight to the Healthy Island card. (Or "to the Blight space", if not playing with a Blight card.)

Most salient questions other than "But why?" can be answered by noting the underlined words. This involves a single piece of plastic being added to the Blight Card, exactly once.

But why?

There's a fencepost error in the Blight system: while the quantity of Blight in the game scales linearlyproportionally wi

1 player = 1 usable Blight
2 players = 3 usable Blight
3 players = 5 usable Blight
4 players = 7 usable Blight

Under the new system:
1 player = 2 usable Blight
2 players = 4 usable Blight
3 players = 6 usable Blight
4 players = 8 usable Blight

....with the rationale being: 
...while the quantity of Blight in the game scales linearly with the number of players, the quantity of usable Blight does not...

But here's where I'm lost:  If Usable Blight is Y and # of players = X, then:

Old System:  Y = 2X - 1
New System: Y = 2X

This is a call/plea/suggestion/request about the possibility of some sort of omnibus rules, a single source for SI rules. 

At least when SI started I always thought of it as a "read the card" game:  A game that had a few basic, intuitive guiding principles, but in which the action was largely governed by reading the cards and doing what they said.

With the addition of "actions," "nested actions," "triggered actions," "action modifiers", and further addition of things like "action trees" and "priority of action modifiers," it seems like the game's complexity has increased exponentially.  We now have rules like this (JE, P. 25):

"Lastly: a few things can initiate base Actions in the middle of other Actions.  In cases like this, you pause the current Action, Resolve the entire new Action-tree (base Action and anything triggered by it, directly or indirectly), then return to the original Action."

The current state of affairs rules-wise seems somewhat disorganized.  To answer a game que

For another example, I just read this off the FAQ:

Can a triggered action trigger itself if it does so via a (nested) basic action? (FAQ) - No. "Can't trigger themselves even indirectly" includes nested actions; otherwise infinite loops would be possible.
A concrete example: Wildfire adds Presence, triggering Damage + Blight. The Blight card flips and is Unnatural Proliferation, whose immediate effects (a basic action) let Wildfire add more Presence. Blazing Presence would not trigger again, because we are still in a chain of actions coming from Blazing Presence.

Reading this immediately raised the following questions:
"...via a (nested) basic action..." Part 1:  -- What is a basic action?  The term is not contained in the base rules or B&C.  The JE rules use the terminology "base action."   You need to go to the FAQ/errata, under the "Nomenclature" section, to see that "base action" is now "basic action."

"...via a (nested) basic action..." Part 2:  -- The FAQ/Errata defines "neste
I would also find something like this extremely helpful, especially with JE and the increased complexity it brings (at least in my mind).

To clarify, are you (collectively -- anyone who has responded so far) more interested in a formal, rules-ese complete rules set with outline numbering, or are you more interested in a rulebook in the more conversational style of the existing rulebooks, albeit with all of the rules and rulings in one document? They'd both be useful, albeit for different use cases.

The idea of a "full/detailed" rulebook is a difficult concept to pin down.

Do you want a rulebook you can read before you start your first game? (You really don't want absolutely everything in such a document)

Do you want a rulebook where all possible details for a concept are in one place?  What order should it be in?  What do you do when concepts appear it multiple places; do need to define it fully in each place it appears?

I get the impression the OP is after a single linear document where all possible rules and FAQs are present, which is not the kind of "rulebook" that would be good place for a person to learn the game from.  That brings to mind Eldritch Horror, which has a "rulebook" that describes the basic structure of the game, and then an "Reference Guide" (Appendix basically) that has the actual full rules for each component/concept in alphabetical order.  The reference guide is absolutely not something someone should read front-to-back to try to understand the game (unle

I'd volunteer, but in all honesty, my eyes glaze over when I start reading about "actions," "triggered actions," "sub-actions," "action modifiers," "action modifier priorities," etc., etc., and the concepts are so unintuitive to me that I wouldn't trust myself to do it properly.

Same. I love this game, but I can't even begin to care about any of those topics. 

I learned  by reading the 3rd edition rules multiple times. I'm not scared of complexity. I just can't see how this game is helped at all by an influx of arcane rules.

To clarify, are you (collectively -- anyone who has responded so far) more interested in a formal, rules-ese complete rules set with outline numbering, or are you more interested in a rulebook in the more conversational style of the existing rulebooks, albeit with all of the rules and rulings in one document?For me, decidedly the former.  I can't speak for everybody else, but in posting the topic, I had two primary concepts in mind:

(1) Single Source.   First and foremost, having all of the "Rules," (as such) in one place.  Even if we consider the FAQ to consist of rule interpretations and not "Rules" with a capital "R," there are still four different sources for the latter:  (1) base game rulebook, (2) B&C additions, (3) JE additions (4) Errata.  Some of these contain content not found in the others.  Some of these contradict the others.  Having a single set of "R"ules rather than having to flip between three different books to find a Rule, then flip to the Errata to make sure that n

For my money, once we started having multiple types of definitions for what constitutes an "action", followed by numerous mechanics that care about actions and their different sorts is when I really lost any ability to keep to the rules as intended.

This might not be a bad idea.

The nice thing about this is that I find it comes up way less often than the quantity of rules would make you expect.  It’s there so when you have a question you can answer it, but the vast majority of the game is still much closer to “read the card” in actual experience, at least as I find it.

The day I remember to place every extra explorer in a land without one for France Level 6 is the day I start worrying about what a nested action is.

In our household we very much just play for fun and only bother to look up a ruling in the FAQ if it seems like we might be cheesing a loophole that makes the game too easy (and/or think we might face the given situation more than once in a blue moon). We largely just favor internal consistency in rules application game to game over 100% technical accuracy. The vast majority of our games do not involve any lookup of the rules, and we've been able to get by by just reading the cards. I can't claim to be following The Rules 100% of the time, but as I said above I know I'm occasionally missing even the basic stuff so I'm not bothered if we parse an action tree slightly wrong. The game's still quite fun.

I believe the first rulebook had a sidebar that suggested just doing what makes sense if you ever encountered a situation that was ambiguous.  It was part of a series of little sections that encouraged players to make the game fun and keep it going smoothly.  I liked that this was in the book.

I don't really understand those rules changes...  All this talk of triggered actions and such, I would expect this from a hyper competitive game like M:TG.  This is a fun if somewhat thinky coop/solo.  Was there really a need for all this legalese?  I was kinda shocked when I got to that section of the JE rulebook.

I feel like 50% of the rules now exist to describe 5% of the possible scenarios.

Don't get me wrong, I still love this game, I just don't really understand the need for all this.  I guess I am not who these rules changes are for.  If someone wants to make a complete rulebook you can go ahead but I think most people will be content to ignore this kind of complexity.  I kind of like t

Adam Kwapinski has been answering some rules questions in the facebook group, so I thought we could start collecting them here for posterity's sake.  Per request, I'm also going to include the official AR clarifications from BGG.  In general, I'm only including clarifications here, not confirmations of something that was written in the rule book.


Actions
Unless specified otherwise on the card (e.g. Scout's Motion Scanner), you must finish an action before starting the next action. Link.

In order to play Interruption, you must be in the same room as the interrupted player. Link Link.

Interruption can be played even if a player has already passed this turn. Link.

If an action card allows you to perform a basic action (e.g. move, shoot) you do not have to discard any additional action cards to pay for the basic action.  You still pay any other cost for the action (e.g. discarding ammo to shoot).

Hey guys! 

Within few next week we will make a full errata with FAQ, as well as we should have up a video-tutorial by Matt form Board Game Replay ; )

New additions:

If you already have a larva on your character board, you do not die if you are attacked by a second larva and infested again. Link.

If the Storage room has a malfunction token, you may search the room using the "Search" action card, but not using the room action.  Using the room action to search does not reduce the item count in the room. Link.

When using a scanning action that scans multiple infection cards, no matter how many cards are "Infected," you only place one Larva miniature on your Character board.  You do not die if you scan multiple "Infected" cards during the same scanning action. Link.

Lots of rules discussion on facebook, but less AR interaction (they seem to be focusing on the rules clarifications over here more, and hopefully that forthcoming FAQ).  New answers:

The light wound track is (as the name implies) a track.  You place a token on the first spot with your first light wound, move it to the second spot with your second light wound, then remove it and gain a serious wound with your third light wound.  3 Light Wounds = 1 Serious Wound. Link.

The blank token is returned to the Intruder bag whenever it is drawn for an encounter, not just if it is the last token in the bag. Link.

One new one, and while doing a TTS playthrough I realized there were some old ones that I missed.

The Coolant Leak event triggers the self destruct timer even if there is already a character in hibernation. Link.

Characters and Intruders who die as a result of the airlock opening do not leave behind corpses.  Everything is vented into space. Link.

Fire spreads into unexplored rooms. Link.

Once the nest is destroyed, it stays destroyed even if an egg is returned to the nest or laid by the queen.  This is why you add an injury marker to the nest. Link.

The Malfunction event typically places a malfunction token in the cockpit.  It is heavily implied (though not explicitly stated) that you place a malfunction token in the lowest numbered explored room without a malfunction token. Link.

Malfunction tokens can be placed in the cockpit, hibernatorium, and engine rooms. Link.

It's lat and maybe I am being dense but I don't understand how the card works. 

Does it actually allow me to copy any production increase from a previously played card for 9 ME?

Thank you.

Greg

Its a known fact that robots work twice as fast as human beings. So, yes, by playing this card you get rid of the slow and lazy crew and your robots will double the production.

Note, robotic workforce doubles everything within a brown box on the target card. In some cases they might double a decrease of production as well!
Also, this card can only target a building card (a project card with a building tag in the top right corner).

This is actually one of the more complex cards in the game. As Carsten states, you copy only the brown box on another card.
My favorite example:
I play Strip Mine (which has a building tag), decreasing my energy production 2 steps, but increasing my steel production 2 steps and my titanium production 1 step. The card also raises the oxygen 2 steps, giving me 2 Terraform Rating.

After that, I play Robotic Workforce. Once again, I decrease energy production 2 steps and increase steel production 2 steps and titanium production 1 step. But this time I do not raise oxygen.
As a follow up question, how does this card interact with building cards that allow placement of special tiles?

Not. Only copies production (brown) boxes.

You're thinking about Mining Rights and Mining Area. The production of those cards depend on the special tile that they also place (giving you production of the cooresponding steel or titanium placement bonus you get for the tile).
If you use Robotic Workforce on for example Mining Rights, you get the same production that you originally got when playing Mining Rights, and thus depending on where that tile was placed.

So if Mining Rights placed its tile on a titanium resource bonus, you got both the titanium bonus resource and 1 step of titanium production. When playing Robotic Workforce, you get another step of titanium production.

Cheers!

- You have an unlimited number of actions each generation, but may only take 1 or 2 at a time (your turn). After the other players’ turns, you get a new turn. Only if you passed (did no action on your turn) you are out and may not have any more turns during that action phase.

- Setup: Choose your starting cards at the same time as you choose your corporation card (Choosing a Beginner corporation must be done before seeing the cards though).

In the interest of helping people play this game solo, I have compiled a bunch of common mistakes that people are making. Feel free to add your own in the comments, I will add them to the list.

Here we go:

1 - Once the Automa can cross rivers it can also use lake hexes as if they were regular hexes (for all units including workers) and will also score end game points for lake hexes it controls.

2 - Automa scores stars for hitting stars on its tracking card, plus reaching full power on the power track, plus up to two combat victories.

3 - Automa never gains or loses popularity.

4 - If executing moves correctly Automa will never have more than one combat unit and/or one worker per hex (i.e. never two mechs, two workers, or a mech and character on the same hex).

5 - Automa can only spend power it has on the track for combat, but can use multiple combat cards even though it will only have one combat unit in a contested hex.

6 - The "skip an Automa turn" symbol is only used for "easy

Here's a short-guide I made to help people understand how the Mill building actually works.

Original wording (pg18):
MILL: Whenever you take the Produce action, the Mill may produce as if it were 1 worker. If there are workers on the Mill territory, they may also produce (it's an extra territory for production).

Better wording (by me):

MILL: Whenever you take the Produce action, the territory with your Mill may count as an extra (bonus) territory for production. The Mill will produce 1 resource (as if it were a worker). If there are actual workers on the Mill territory, they may also produce resources.

If still confused, this is a detailed breakdown of the definition:
The Mill structure essentially provides two optional effects when you take the Produce action on your turn.
1.) The hex the Mill structure is on counts as a free tile to produce on. Produce on that tile following normal rules of production.
2.) The Mill structure itself will produce 1 resource (or 1 worker if the tile

Rulebook: “In as situation where the pawn is in the middle of the board, the player who begins the next Age is the last active player.”

Helpsheet: “The player with the weakest military decides which player begins the Age. In case of a tie, it's the player who went last in the previous Age who chooses.”

So in case of a tie does the last player begin the next Age or choose who begins the next Age?
Good catch. We hardly ever have a military tie, and in that case we had the person who did not end the previous era play first.

Hum, I have the italian edition and there's not mention of the thing in the helpsheet, and I can't find it even in the english one - http://www.7wondersduel.com/files/HELP/7-Wonders-Duel-Helpsheet-US.pdf , are we talking about the same helpsheet?
It looks like a different version of the helpsheet indeed. I'd go with the rulebook.

Agreed.
I'm starting to think that I have a counterfeit copy of the game :D
You begin the age by choosing whether you go first or second, I see no contradiction.

You begin the age by choosing whether you go first or second, I see no contradiction.
The contradiction is that choosing whether you go first is not the same as going first.

As the OP notes, the English rulebook says “In a situation where the pawn is in the middle of the board, the player who begins the next Age is the last active player.” There is no choosing implied by that: it says that the player begins the next Age. It does not say that the player chooses who begins the next Age.


FWIW, the published Polish version of the rules agrees with the published English rules (i.e. it says that when military is tied, then whoever did the last action in the previous round starts the next round).

Well spotted indeed. I have send this question to Repos Production to get an official answer.

And I have the answer to this question :)

If the conflict pawn is in the middle of the military track at the end of an Age, the player who took the last card of that Age begins the following Age. That player doesn't have the choice.

When there is no tie in military, the player who is currently losing on the military track may decide who begins the following Age.

Hope this clarifies it.

Am I understanding it correctly that if I grab for example Magistrates Guild and I have 3 blue cards, but my opponent has 5 blue cards, then I get 5 coins and in the end of the game it will be worth 5 points (if my opponent still has 5 blue cards and I still have less than 5 blue cards) ?

Conversely, if I have 7 blue cards and my opponent has 5 blue cards, I get 7 coins and its worth 7 points in the end if number of blue cards dont change.
Yes, that's right. The guild cards score (coints and points) according to either you or your opponent's city, depending on which has the most red cards, coins etc.

You understood it correctly.

Immediately and only once the guild is built in your city, you gain 1 coin for each blue card in the city that has the most (5 coins in your first example and 7 in your second).

At the end of the game you gain 1 VP for each blue card in the city that has the most, this number might have been changed during the course of game since the guild has been built. Example:
- When you build the guild, you have 5 blue cards and your opponent has 4. You immediately gain 5 coins one-off.
- Before the end of the game your opponent built 3 more blue cards, now they have 7 and you still have 5. You gain 7 VP from Magistrates Guild.

As folks are getting their 2nd edition copies there seems to be a resurgence of questions about Monster AI. I thought I'd start a quiz for people to test their understanding. Most of these questions are based on similar or identical ones from posts on the old FAQ:
https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1687146/official-faq-old

Feel free to add to these, discuss, or disagree about answers. I'm not really an expert.

For all questions:
M = Monster
C = Player character
C1 has lower/faster initiative than C2, etc.
Brown hex = Obstacle
Green "T" hex = damage trap
Black = wall
White = open hex
Assume attacks are melee and also Monsters do not have Flying unless otherwise indicated.

(I'm posting questions one at a time since I couldn't get the quiz maker to work with multiple questions.)

Update
Sadgit has converted this quiz into a Geek List: Gloomhaven Rules Quiz

It includes all of these questions with the updated answers to questions 10 and 12, plus a couple bonus questions. Thanks, Sadgit!

Question 1


Explanation of answer:
To get to its target, M1 has to move 3 hexes to either the hex NW or NE of C1. Moving to "a" or "b" shortens that path to 2 hexes, so it does so.
 Hex "a" and "b" are equivalent so players can choose which one it goes to.

Explanation:
What makes this different than question 1 is that the shortest path for M1 to attack its target is to move 3 hexes through its allies to the hex directly north of C1. Moving to "a" or "b" results in it still being 3 hexes away from its target. Since this is no closer (and it can't land on the hex with M2) it doesn't move.

Explanation:
M1 first chooses its focus. It takes 2 movement to get to either C1 or C2, so the tie-breaker is whichever enemy is closer "by the crow flies", not counting obstacles. C2 is closer by this measure, so M1 focuses on C2. (Initiative is only used as a second tie-breaker, which isn't needed here.) Since "a" and "b" are equivalent, players choose.

Explanation:
The shortest path for M1 to get to its target (and also the only path that doesn't spring a trap) is to move 3 hexes through its allies to the hex north of C1. Since it can't get there, or even shorten that path, with the 2 movement it has, it stays put.

Explanation:
M1 cannot move through its enemy C1. Nor can it stand where M3 is to attack. So its only path to the target is the long way around through the trap. It shortens that path as much as it can with its movement, which puts it on the trap. Sorry about that, M1.

Explanation:
This is similar to the previous question in that there is no path for M1 to get to its target other than the long way around. Again M3 is in its way. So rather than heading in a direction that it can't attack from 
 ("c"), it embarks on the long journey around the obstacles. Since both the east and west route are 11 hexes long, they are equivalent and players can choose which path it takes.
This would be great as a Geeklist so that discussion can be focused on particular questions.

Explanation:
This setup is superficially similar to question 4, with the key difference that the path through M1's allies is now blocked by an obstacle. The only hex from which M1 can attack is 2 hexes north of C1, from where it can range C1 across the obstacle. And the only path to get to that spot is through the trap.

I second this.. :whistle:

Yeah please restart this as a geeklist and provide the link on this thread when you do.

Explanation:
The rules state that a monster will maximize its attack on its primary target before worrying about other targets. In this case its primary focus is C2, since C2 is closest to it. M1 will therefore prioritize attacking C2 without disadvantage over being able to hit a third target (C3). The only way for M1 to hit all three targets AND make sure it hits C2 without disadvantage is to stand on the trap. However, monsters will only stand on a trap if there is no other way to focus on an enemy, which doesn't apply here. (There is another reason M1 would not stand there, but I'll save that for later.) So M1 gives up on hitting C3 this time. As for C1 and C2, there is only one spot where M1 can attack both of them without disadvantage and that is "b".
On question 3, why doesn't it attack C1? The characters are equidistant so the monster will attack the lowest initiative.

• In this phase, remove the leftmost building resource (i.e. closest to the arrow) from each face-up mountain strip and return it to the general supply.

If all spaces but the last “2 silver” space are empty, remove the two silver and the entire mountain strip.

As far as I can tell there are two reasonable interpretations of the rule above:


A) That the second paragraph is an additional, follow-up instruction: if, after removing a resource (e.g. Ore), the only one left is the last "2 silver", you also remove it and the Mountain Strip:

i.e. 'If all spaces but the last "2 silver" are then empty, also remove the two silver and the entire mountain strip'. (This was the way MiWi played in his excellent walkthrough video)

B) That it is just a slightly clumsy way of saying that once you empty the Mountain Strip (by removing the final "2 silver") you also remove the Mountain Strip:

i.e. 'If all spaces but the last “2 silver” space are empty at the start of the phase, remove the two silver

I can't say with certainty which is correct, but I had been playing the game in Excel quite a few times just to see how it plays, and I played it assuming A was correct. Now that I reread it, B does seem to make more sense.

If B is correct a better way of saying it would had been something like.

"If all spaces are empty remove the entire mountain strip."

B) is correct

No. Silver is a source of points, not just something to cover negatives. So if you end the game with 59 silver, that’s 59 points. Which means if I cover all my negatives with blue and green tiles, and have 59 silver as well, I am 59 points to the good. The scoresheet works pretty well as far as that goes, you simply add up all the positives (houses, cards, silver, islands, animals), then subtract all the negatives still visible on your boards.

My experience is that people tend to irrational place all silver on -1vp places to avoid minus points (phychological reason) even if this doesn't change anything. For making it sometimes a difference I added step by step -2vp spaces, so in lack of enough silver/ore to cover this would hurt and you have a good reason to cover than.

I went through the rule book and pulled together a list of rules that weren't obvious, were flat-out exceptions not spelled out in the Learn to Play or otherwise were important to know.

Rules from the RR that were not in the L2P:
-Reshuffle Tactics discard piles back into their decks at the end of combat 

-Separate reroll abilities may reroll the same dice multiple times 

-If the Imperial player’s only remaining ship is the Death Star Under Construction and the Rebel player still has ships in the system, the Death Star Under Construction is destroyed.

-During the retreat step, if the only Rebel ships in the combat are Rebel Transports, they must retreat or they are immediately destroyed. 

-May pass even if there are still unrevealed missions. Missions not revealed return to hand at end of Command Phase and their leaders return to pool 

-Any Rebel player may voluntarily reveal the base during their turn in the Command Phase 

-Rebel Base is revealed only if Imperial *Ground* troop

The Rebel ships are forced to retreat at the end of a combat
round if all of the following conditions are true:
I. The only Imperial ship in the system is a Death Star,
which cannot roll dice because there are two or
more Ion Cannons in the system.

III. The Rebels did not play a “Death Star Plans”
objective card at some time during that combat
round.

During the Ground Battle Round

Rebel Transports, though, auto-destruct at the end of the retreat step if the conditions apply.

1659714.body:
Hi all,

I've played the game twice now (love it) and both times we've come to have to interpret a rule: when you move your train forward, as a reward, it is possible to move it forward zero spaces?

Please note that it is not the same as giving up the reward entirely - at least not if you're in a train station.

Let's say I move into a train station for the first time on a given turn, but have no money or desire to upgrade it. I may have moved there just to prevent other players from doing so (I am that kind of player).
Fast forward a bit, and I can move the train forward again: if I can move it forward zero spaces, leaving it where it is, and if I have the cash ready this time, then I can upgrade the station. Unless of course there is a minimum movement of one space, but the rules don't say so; however, they don't say you can stay put either.

Please leave your opinions, and if you are entitled, write your clarifications.

Yes, you can move 0 steps. And therefore yes, if you stop your movement in a station, you may build it.

Edit: Just spoke to the editor Viktor, who did a whole bunch of testing. He prefers that "stop movement" implies moving at least 1 space. So in the next print run we will clarify the rules in this respect. Please play it this way, that you have to move at least 1 space to build a station.

Thank you for the very fast clarification. For all it's worth, I'm glad to say we had guessed correctly and played accordingly both times.

But I have one more question! I'll start a separate post though.

Edit: following your edit, it appears that we had NOT guessed correctly after all. Ah well, I enjoyed it while it lasted.
But don't worry: I'll blame Viktor, not you.

Wow - I read the original reply and never bothered to check for edits, so I missed the reversal. The situation even occurred in game since and I convinced everybody to allow it because "the designer himself said so on BGG". :p

Phase A of a player's turn requires moving the cowboy at least one space, so it makes sense that an action to move a train would also require a move of at least one space. This seems consistent to me.

However, if the player has unlocked any auxiliary action(s) that requires moving the train backwards, then the player whose train is already in a station could use a building that provides both train movement and an auxiliary action to move their train backward and then forward in the same turn, returning to the same station. If they did not have the money to upgrade the station on their previous turn, it is unlikely that they would have the money on their next turn. It is possible, though, if they receive a "hand" payment from another player.

Hello Phil,

It's probably clear to you, but still safe to point out that movement in phase A is mandatory, while the reward part of an action can be forfeited; therefore, I may have an action to move my train engine forward, but decline to carry it out and leave the train where it is; however, if I do so, as clarified by Viktor and Alexander, I must also decline the opportunity to place my token on the station where my train is.

Also please note that I can keep my train "parked" in a station for several turns - not just by refusing to move my train, but simply because I happen to land on tiles that never have an action to do so; therefore, I may have several and various chances to raise money to be able to place a token in the station where my train has been idling - if only the rules allowed me to do so.

This should be a rather rare occurrence, but then, it happened during my second game (and I haven't had a third game yet).

A player had built his 5a building: that's the building that allows you to hire a worker for a 1 coin discount.
He then landed on this building and used that action to get his fourth builder: this triggered the immediate action to erect/replace a building for half the normal cost - and he decided to replace the very 5a building he was on for a "bigger" one.

Again, this must be a rare occurrence and I might not see it happen again, but a clarification won't hurt.
We assumed that the building replacement would kick in at the end of the player's turn; therefore, for the rest of that turn, he was allowed to use the other action on his 5a building (he hadn't yet), but he was not allowed to use any actions from the building that replaced it.
Was our decision correct?

Please share your opinions, or leave clarifications if entitled.
You played it correct: Don't use the new building, but complete all actions of the replaced building.

Many thanks again for another very quick reply.

Awesome game, by the way.

We use a D8 to randomize building selections 3 at a time.
Use the result D8-1 to get a number 0-7. You now have a single digit octal number which you convert to binary.

1 (or odds) = A side
0 (or evens) = B side.
If you don't know binary:
0 = 000 = BBB
1 = 001 = BBA
2 = 010 = BAB
3 = 011 = BAA
4 = 100 = ABB
5 = 101 = ABA
6 = 110 = AAB
7 = 111 = AAA

Do this 3 times for the first 9 buildings.
A final roll of even/odd determines the final 10th building.

If this is not nerdy enough for you and you have 3 different colored D8s that just happen to be lying around, then you can choose a color combination that your remember like RGB (red, green, blue) and roll the 3 D8s and a D6 all at once to determine the whole building randomness. As a bonus, if everyone can convert to binary in their heads, you don't even have to tell anyone how to set their buildings. The dice tell you.

This is probably the nerdiest way to select buildings until someone makes a d1024.

I would say that this is defiantly the most complicated setup to the game that I have seen. 

Is it more nerdy to roll dice or write code to do it for you? I spent a few hours encoding small pictures and randomization code so that I can have an unbiased game setup. It even chooses the player order randomly (if you pick colors before randomizing).

2047763.body: I've played two games of Everdell now, and both times we had the rules for Meadow cards wrong. I've just now come to realize this. I'm now reading on page 9 of the rule book where cards can either be "played" from hand or from the Meadow. However, it was the rules about "drawing" cards from the Meadow on page 10 that confused me. Both games, very few Meadow cards came into play, unless done so by another card, a forest action space or the end of summer. Now I see that you can always "play" a card from the Meadow. While I have enjoyed both plays of this game very much, this new detail (new-to-me) changes so much. I hope others aren't making the same mistake.

It was fairly clear that Meadows Cards are shared between players :D. Now you will see how the gameplay can really change in a better way!
Consider, then, that the first player to advance in summer can pick 2 Meadows Cards and "stole" them to the other players before anyone else ;)

2276050.body:
Hello to all Everdell enthusiasts!

You are about to get your paws on a great game and yes, you will have questions.
(The designer, James A. Wilson, and Brenna from Starlings have been very active and answer many questions we all had at a point or another. Now with Gen Con approaching, my guess is that they will be very busy.)

The overall game:

Player A gets twigs
Player B gets a pebble

Player A gets Resin
Player B builds a Crane

Player A builds a Farm and gets 1 berry
Player B discards Crane and builds a Mine and gets 1 pebble

Player A uses an Occupied token and gets a Wife
Player B gets twigs

Player A gives 1 berry to get the Innkeeper
Player B gives twig and pebble to build the Barge

Player A Prepares for Season.
Spring Season: collect 1 Meeple and Activate all Production (Green) cards in your city.: Player A has a Farm in the city so the Farm gives Player A 1 berry. Player A only has 1 Production card to activate. Player A is now in Spring.
Player B uses an Occupied Token on

Also

Pay attention to open/shared (semi-circle) and closed (circle) locations.

Reveal means you will draw cards for an effect (like gaining coins), you may even build one of them in some cases (postal pigeon, cemetery) but you will have to discard the rest unless specified otherwise.

Draw is gaining cards and keeping them in your hand (hand limit still counts)

Remember that when you Prepare for Summer, you draw cards from the Meadow.


Remember that you only get one action per turn. 

If you build a construction, you have to wait for a future turn to get the matching critter.
You do not have to get the matching critter if you do not want. 
They do NOT share the same space than their construction. And a construction and a critter do not have to be side by side. You can build multiple things before getting the matching critter.

Adding one thing.
The deck is what is face down, under the tree.
The Meadow is the board area with 8 face up cards.
You can play a card from the Meadow, you can sometimes even Draw from the Meadow: Prepare for Summer, Undertaker, Forest Location.

The Discard pile is face down. In the rare instance you will draw from the Discard, you draw from top of the Discard pile downward.

2280192.body:
An embarrassing tale (all the more so because I was involved with playtesting the two new expansions) that I tell in the off chance that there's one other person reading who's made the same mistake...

Yesterday we were having our first game of Pearlbrook, and I was pointing out to my daughter the fact that there is one shared space on the River board, and three exclusive spaces, and I gestured towards the full/complete circles that enabled us to remember that. My daughter then said "But doesn't that mean that some of these basic locations should be shared too?" pointing at the two wood and a card space, the one resin space and the one berry space.

My husband and I's eyes went towards those basic locations and saw that, yes indeed their circles were incomplete. For 52 games we had played that all the basic locations were exclusive, we'd never noticed that half had open circles! Jaws were dropped and heads were shaken in disbelief. For all those games we'd been playing on hard mode, wi

Honestly, my wife and I did the same thing.  Not for 52 games but definitely for 10 games or so.  We had not played for a bit and I gave the rules a re-read and noticed that when re-reading the rules.  

Funny but the game seems to play just fine either way.

I didn't make this mistake, but I've actually been considering house ruling that those spaces are exclusive in 2 player games just to tighten the board up that little bit more.  Glad to know it works just fine that way.  :laugh:

As I always say when I screw up board game rules: "It wasn't a mistake, it was a house rule."  ;)

I do feel a fool (and should be given -2 points) for staring at the board for 52 games and never spotting those open circles on half the basic locations.:blush::cry:

Here's a list of repeated misconceptions and mistakes I've seen in my own FtF games as well as read about here on BGG.

Misinterpretation of rules:
- charge power from bowl II to bowl III even though there are still power tokens in bowl I (mainly for players without previous TM exposure)
- forget to subtract victory points when charging two or more power
- expect to gain a tech tile when spending four knowledge to advance on a tech track
- ignore the requirement of flipping a federation tile to advance to level 5 on a research track
- ignore the requirement of flipping a federation tile to take an advanced tech tile
- ignore the requirement of covering a standard tech tile when taking an advanced tech tile

Other common errors:
- forget to take the income from Economy research (and maybe even from tech tiles and/or round boosters)
- forget to advance on a research track when taking an advanced tech tile

- expect to gain a tech tile when spending four knowledge to advance on a tech track

It doesn't matter how many times I reiterate the correct rules, this continues to be a point of confusion among people I've explained the game to (and I'm widely regarded as an excellent rules teacher).

The mistake is always the same: someone on level 3 of a tech track thinks they can build a scientific structure, move up to level 4 and then take the advanced tech tile. Someone actually kept getting confused (and extremely frustrated when told he couldn't do this) on THREE separate occasions.

I've since decided that in addition to explaining the rules, I'm going to go over this specific situation.

If you have any questions about forming a Federation in Gaia Project. Please check this FAQ first.





First follow these steps when forming a federation. I like to call them the "three rules". 


Rule 1: Choose. First pick out the planets you wish to join into a federation, they must total in power value of at least 7. 

Rule 2: Link. Next, place satellites (usually by discarding power tokens) to link the chosen planets together using the least amount of satellites possible. No planet NOR satellite of the newly formed federation can be directly adjacent to planets OR satellites from any of your existing federations.

2469057.body:
(A decade ago, I put together a version of this for original Brass.  For those of you who need it and haven't surfed the Lancs forums, I update it for Birmingham players here. 
Credit due to  and  for suggesting beer-related updates.) 
 Original thread: https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/680754/

A number of people have commented that while the connection and card rules may be thematic, they're too complicated and too confusing. While Brass is a tricky game to teach, explaining these rules in-theme makes them actually comprehensible. Here's my approach:

0. Contrary to the map, the Midlands did actually have a functioning road network (hey, there's a cart wheel right there on the cover!). But carting large, heavy loads of goods by road isn't a profitable way to do business*, so it turns out only iron cubes, and sometimes beer, can move on the (invisible) roads.

1. Coal is needed in such huge quantities that you can't do business without a coal source connected by canal or rail to the bu

I also usually explain that after you build a tile, somebody gets left in charge of running the place. That ambitious young fellow or lady is going to do the best they can to turn a profit, finding a buyer for whatever product they make. So if another player can use that coal, iron, beer; then that contract gets signed without your input, while you're off surveying your next project.  The money you make in these sales is abstracted into income steps when the tile flips.
Ive been thinking about how to intro this to the wife and this seems like a good bet! Better than rules anyway!

The Timing section of the RRG on page 2 is incomplete.

All timing conflicts in the Action Phase are resolved in Initiative Order starting with the Active Player.  The timing section of the RRG neglects to mention that it starts with the Active Player.

It also neglects to mention that you should use clockwise from Speaker order in the Agenda Phase.

Essentially, rules 2.9 and 2.10 should be used for all timing conflicts of abilities, not just the play of action cards.

So it seems to me that the Arborec’s build abilities are probably the number one most-asked question on BGG and FFG. There’s a lot of different questions, and they’re scattered around the boards, with lots of conflicting answers in the comments.

What I hope to do here is write a definitive list of questions, and the answers to each, based on community consensus. I’m playing with Arborec on Sunday, so want to make sure that I have things right.

If you disagree with any of the answers below (or any new questions that I missed!), please let everyone know in the comments with reasons why, and I will update the OP (with credits of course!)

ARBOREC FAQ

A1: Can Arborec pool their Letani build capacity?
YES. For Example, with two Letani Warriors on a planet, you can produce two more Letani or two fighters for a total cost of one resource.

A2: Can Arborec pool Letani + Space Dock capacity?

Its true there has been a number of arborec and letani questions, so a thread summary on the matter is in order. Good idea.

Just a few minor notes:

Can Arborec pool Letani + Space Dock capacity?
YES. But you can still only produce more Letani up to what your Letani production limit allows. For example, if you had one Space Dock and one Letani (I) on a planet, you could only produce one more Letani for a total cost of one resource (expensive!), and the rest of the units produced would have to be ships.

Hey everyone! Welcome to the FAQ thread. You'll find lots of useful stuff here.

Latest FAQ
First and foremost, if you're looking for more answers to common questions, you'll find our FAQ here.

Latest Law of Root
If you have a rules question, the first thing I'd recommend is reading the Law of Root, especially the first few couple chapters—they include important context for understanding the rules structure of Root. You can find the latest version of the Law of Root in the Resources section of our site here.

Old Rulings
You can find many answers to questions by searching for a related thread on BGG, or you can start your own and ask away! However, be careful if you’re reading a thread started before June 2018, since you may be reading about a rule that existed in a pre-release version of the game. Likewise, a couple rulings have changed in the 8th Printing / Marauder Expansion because of changes done to support new content; you can find these changes by searching for an asterisk (*)

I love teaching Root. It's not just to get people into this favorite game of mine, but also because I think the game really needs a teacher in order for players to 'get it'. I've seen folks struggle for an hour trying to understand it, and I feel compelled to rush in and save them.

In many ways Root is pretty straightforward; players can pick up their factions' thing in one rotation. But in teaching I'm burdened by a number of "Gotcha" rules hiding in the Law that come up infrequently enough to be annoying. They rear their heads typically after players have done a thing, or after they've strategized and are in the middle of a thing. I feel a little embarrassed misleading them and think I haven't been teaching them adequately when this comes up.

So, as a cheat-sheet for me and others, I thought about compiling this list with uncommon rules facts I know for others learning the game. This is to complement the helpful FAQ thread here and the official FAQ. Feel free to correct me before I

Thank you for clarifying the vagabond sidebar items, I usually teach the game but never play vagabond and think I have been too nice!
Also good point on round tokens not counting for rule.
Useful list. Thanks.

+ In combat, the attacking player scores a point for each token (not warrior, but square and round tokens) removed.
Since game text distinguishes between "buildings" and "tokens," I always refer to them collectively as "cardboard."


+ You can only improve your relationship with a chosen faction once a turn.
You can. You just can't count an aid action twice. If you aid a faction six times in a turn, you can go from Indifferent to Allied.


+ Your actions are revealed cards. Any cards you do not reveal should be used to discard for scoring. Discarded cards go to the Lost Souls pile.
The procedure for scoring is "reveal and discard a card," not "reveal a card, then discard a different card." This is somewhat ambiguous in the original Law, but has been clarified in the FAQ thread. Not sure how the latest version of the Law looks.

+ In combat, the attacking player scores a point for each token (not warrior, but square and round tokens) removed.BOTH players score a point for each token removed (not just the attacker).  Rare, but possible (with an ambush, Vagabond help, Vagabond, etc.).  

Also, hostile vagabond attackers DO score for killing warriors (this is not mentioned in the Vagabond section, but should be).

>> Eyrie must pay attention to this as it may cause them to go into turmoil if they cannot move out of a clearing they do not rule.They can always move INTO a clearing they rule, so I'm not sure why you differentiate here.

+ In order to place a building you must rule the clearing with the wood, and all subsequent clearings connected to where you are trying to build to. Including the one you're building IN.

+ Field Hospitals saves all cats present in a battle. They immediately go to the Keep and not into Coffin Makers (E&P deck). Field hospitals work for Woodland Alliance Revolts and Crow Bombs as well

+ Be careful about Rule, as you may only move From clearings that you rule, and build within clearings that you rule. The Lizard cult is going to be the Eyrie's worst enenmy in this regard since an Eyrie player will have to dig through those warriors in order to get to the clearing space.

Birds follow normal move rules, they can move from a clearing they do not rule to a clearing they rule.  The decree specifies which clearing they must live from, but they do not need to rule that clearing if they rule the clearing they are moving to.

I remember Outrage for moving Warriors (mainly because that the Vagabond isn't a warrior, they don't cause Outrage) but I almost always forget that removing a Sympathy Token causes it too.

+ When you are moving, it must be to or From a clearing you rule. The only exception to this is the Crows per one of their berry abilities, or a crafted card from exiles and partisans (??).

I'm pretty sure the otters can move along the river regardless of rule. Also the vagabond is a "pawn" not a "warrior" so this does not apply to him either.

Usually. However, if Hostile warriors are in the Vagabond's destination clearing it costs an extra boot token to move there.

Ah, wow, you get points for tokens, too, and not just buildings? I think we may have overlooked that until now (although I'm not 100% sure). :shake:

I'd mention the favor cards and the devastating (and potentially game-winning) effects they can have - they stand apart from the other crafting cards for me. 

You don't want someone to have one sprung on them without knowing the effects, or not to be aware of what someone with the ability to craft three times in mouse / rabbit / fox could do. Similalrly, concentrating your buildings / tokens in one type of clearing can leave you vulnerable.
