Root is a fantastic asymmetrical game with 8 completely different factions competing over the race to 30 victory points. The artwork is amazing, and the asymmetrical part makes the game so much re-playable. 

Perhaps, the biggest drawback of the game is that there are so many minor rules that are either confused or easily missed by beginners, here is the compiled list of rules that you might probably miss 

General rules

- The factions are set up in the order described in the rule book, but any player can start first, going clockwise order.

- When the Lizard is present, all discarded and spent cards by every player, including the dominance card, must go to the lost soul pile first, and these cards will move from lost souls piles to the discard pile during the Birdsong of the Lizard's turn.

- When Vagabond is NOT present, you still need to set up ruins, and the ruins remain forever in the game, depriving a building slot in every clearings they are in.

I'm a bit disappointed if this is the rulebook to be printed, as it doesn't work very well when references don't match up (and the Root rulebook depends heavily on those references).

Also the Vagabond can no longer make a coalition with a player already in coalition.I'm not sure why they made this change.  The only thing it does is prevent 2x Vagabonds from separately forming a coalition with a losing player, but this can still happen if Vagabond #1 joins Vagabond #2 and THEN Vagabond #2 joins player 3 (who is NOT yet in a coalition).  

If Vagabond #2 is already in a coalition with Vagabond #1 how could he join player 3 in another one?

Also the Vagabond can no longer make a coalition with a player already in coalition.I'm not sure why they made this change.  The only thing it does is prevent 2x Vagabonds from separately forming a coalition with a losing player, but this can still happen if Vagabond #1 joins Vagabond #2 and THEN Vagabond #2 joins player 3 (who is NOT yet in a coalition).  

If Vagabon #2 is already in a coalition with Vagabond #1 how could he join player 3 in another one?
Because Vagabond #1 is the one who previously played the dominance/coalition card, while Vagabond #2 is still scoring normally.  The rules do NOT say that a player already in a coalition cannot play a dominance/coalition card, just that they cannot join a coalition with someone that is already in one.  Vagabond #1 is joining player #3, who is NOT in a coalition and is thus a valid target.

I won't bury the lede here: I believe Advanced Setup is a really terrible name for Advanced Setup. 

Because it's likely making you hesitant to try it. Which is what I'm here to try and change today.

… 

OK, perhaps "terrible" is too strong a word, but I will go to great lengths to argue it is at least counterproductive. This revamping of the setup rules, introduced on 2022's Marauder Expansion, was clearly designed to re-balance a game that had grown to a much larger scope than initially anticipated by the original back-of-the-faction-board rules in the base game. As such, I believe the aim of the design couldn't have been other than for it to be used by as many players as possible. Framing it as "Advanced", however, makes it sound much scarier than it should be perceived by players who never used it. In fact, much scarier than it is. 

That's why, if I could change a single thing about Root, big or small, my change would come down to this single word: out with "Advanced", in with "N

I like the way you suggest dipping your toe into adset with your play group to try it out. But you can go even further!

With my current group (who are enjoying the game up into their 4th & 5th play but are still mostly learning all the expansion factions), I have started introducing adset by simply introducing one or two mechanics from adset at a time. Last time, we didn't do a proper n+1 cards draft, or do a homelands / alternate (buffed) setup for any of the factions, but we did select our factions starting with the last player in turn order, alongside immediately setting up after choosing. In our second game of the day, I implemented the deal-five-choose-three hand set-up.

While the rules of adset are fairly easy to explain, I find that even ignoring faction strength & pick / counter-pick strategy the tactical considerations that adset opens up are fairly complex, especially when used with randomized clearing suits. By introducing the rules to people piecemeal, they can spend a bi

I haven't found it as "teach" friendly overall with new players, so I try my best not to use ADSET in people's first game experiences. One aspect that distinguishes Standard setup versus ADSET, is a brand new player has no idea what optimal placement decisions, turn order & matchup considerations to utilize ADSET to the level that experienced players have. So just "out-of-the-box", with people who've never played or experienced Root or even COIN games; I have found it just asks to much of a new player.

I have also found in tables where I have one or two experienced people push ADSET as the "only way to go", when attempting to teach a new player; the underlying reasoning, seems to be more for their personal enjoyment/benefit rather than consider how front-loaded it can be for someone who has no experience with these type of games.

I emailed lautapelit.fi with some rules queries, and they kindly supplied the answers as follows:


Q. Order of drawing reputation tiles after combat - If a player controls a sector but their ships entered last, in what order are reputation tiles drawn after combat in that sector? The rulebook states that reputation tiles are drawn in order of entry, but is unclear on whether the Defender exception applies for this purpose.

A. The player controlling the sector is always counted to have entered first.


Q. Claiming discovery tiles - If a player attacks Ancients and destroys both the Ancients and their own ships at the same time with Rift Cannons, the discovery tile is left unclaimed in that sector. If a player later does an influence action to take control of that sector, do they immediately get the discovery tile? If a player moves a ship to that sector without taking control of it, do they get the discovery tile at that moment, or at the end of the combat phase?

A. Great question! D

Rulebook states that: "At the end of the Combat Phase, if you have at least one Ship in a Sector with a Discovery Tile, take the tile." This would mean that you dont get the tile by the Influence action.

So the only way to pick a tile is to have a ship. You can control the system but still not have the tile? This is very counter-intuitive and not in the spirit of the original game. This requires validation from the author.
I have replied seeking clarification and they said they are passing my question on to the designer. I will keep you posted.

Hey guys,

I've just gotten my copy of the game and we played our first game yesterday.
Some things weren't clear during the game, so we played by hunch, but today I've taken another detailed look at the rules, and I thought I'd share a list of things with you of what we got and played wrong:
1. Non-automatic hits do as much damage as listed on the die "burst" face
  - For some reason, I thought that if I got a "5" on a blue die, but was a hit after all (due to a +1 Computer), that it deals only one damage. But it actually deals 3 damage!
2. Draw multiple, but take only one Reputation tile after battle
  - We kept all drawn tiles by mistake after battle
3. Sector hexes don't need to form wormhole connections on both sides of all edges. It's enough to form a wormhole connection only on the edge of the hex it's connecting to (Wormhole Generator is an exception). Other edges could have a wormhole on one side and a blank on the other
  - I thought that a hex must fit perfectly in the zone

Those first games can be tricky indeed 🙂 
I always forget to advance the roundmarker.................
A good list. Something we got wrong for the first few times: you must assign each combat die rolled to one enemy ship. At first we were just summing up the dice.

The connections end up being a big deal for the more turtle style races. If the turtler (planta/draco) explorers, they can often orient the tile to block access from a more aggressive nieghbor. The aggressors (orion/terran/eridani) will be looking to build routes to thier softer neighbors earlier on.

Those first games can be tricky indeed 🙂 
I always forget to advance the roundmarker.................
I feel you. Our first plays were at night; by midnight it was really easy to forget to move the marker and then wonder why the game was taking so long 😬

While I have always played and explained it like they do, no version of the rules seems to make this explicit and RAW I seem to be able to make the choice for each ship class separately when I choose to have them begin their retreat.

Could you verify for me that it is intended to work this way?

You are right in th
Ships of the same class can move towards different sectors if there is more than one controlled sector available. You move each individual ship towards the sector it is trying to retreat to.

Ships of the same class can move towards different sectors if there is more than one controlled sector available. You move each individual ship towards the sector it is trying to retreat to.

Well ... so far I would not have believed you to be correct.

Time: 15-20 mins (excluding Q&A)

1. Set the scene, letting them know who we are and what’s happening at a high level.
2. Talk about how the market works.
3. Talk about two core actions (buy card, play card).
4. Talk about the tableau when playing card and the immediate effects on the top right of each court card.
5. Discuss each of those effects, which leads into the coalitions. Show actual examples on the map. 
6. Explain loyalty to a coalition and how patriots can change it. 
7. Show that there are supplemental/permanent actions on the bottom of the court cards. You can either in-depth these actions for a complete teach or ask your player's to refer to the player aids. Talk about the four climates, how they get changed and how they provide bonus actions. Explaining the court cards leads into discussion of other forms of loyalty like prizes and gifts. 
8. Talk about dominance cards as part of the market draw and discuss failed check and successful check. Discuss victory conditions at

The rule says “If there is a tie, add up the victory points for the tied places and then divide that number by the number of tied players (rounding down).” What adding needs to be done? Isn’t it just 3 points for first place, 1 for second? So a tie for first between 2 players would just be 3/2, rounded down. So 1 point per player.

Isn’t it just 3 points for first place, 1 for second? So a tie for first between 2 players would just be 3/2, rounded down. So 1 point per player.

But the example right after reads “e.g. two players tied for first place will both score two points ((3+1)÷2).” That +1 is killing me. I’m sure it’s obvious, but I’m lost. Help! :)

First place gets 3 points. Second place gets 1. In a tie you add together first place and second place points, then divide in half. So 3+1, then divide in half. So, 2.

On a failed dominance check, you compare cylinders.

First place would score 3
Second place would score 1

Player A and B are tied for first place, the others are far behind.

That means that A and B are taking up both the first (3 points) and second places (1 point), for a total of 4, which is shared between them.

When radicalizing, Wakhan only considers cards that Wakhan can purchase (apart from whether or not a Dominance Check is in the market).

Zero is a valid choice for "most tribes+spies/armies+roads/rupees".

"Valid choice" includes everything except cards Wakhan cannot afford, Public Withdrawal, Dominance Check, cards covered with rupees this turn, and empty slots.

There are situations in which there is no valid choice for a radicalize. On a second radicalize with no rupees, the one card in column 0 that wasn't covered with a rupee or purchased might be Public Withdrawal or a Dominance Check. So a default radicalize can end up being skipped, and Wakhan does not necessarily always have two actions to take.

Leverage counts when looking for "net the most rupees".

Wakhan's Move counts ALL tribes in the destination region when deciding how many armies to move (but only player tribes when deciding whether or not to move).

I found creating the flowchart helpful in understanding Wakhan rules and understanding where more clarifications were needed. I also didn't try to answer every question in mine (e.g. how to interpret Radicalize when there are specific instructions).

One action:
Buy a Dominance Check if possible and it scores Wakhan the most VPs, OR
If the action listed is anything other than a simple "radicalize", if conditions are met AND it can affect the game state (Wakhan will battle a spy on a Safe House), then perform the action, otherwise go to the next instruction on the card.
OR radicalize:
Tiebreakers go in the order of cheapest, then highest card number.
If Dominance Check is present and there is a dominant coalition, radicalize a matching Patriot, otherwise, radicalize card with most armies+roads.
If Dominance Check is present and no coalition is dominant, radicalize a card with most spies+tribes.
Otherwise default radicalize: Use red/black arrows, following instructions to move along the row to the left, then switch rows and reset column and move along the row to the left, until you reach a "valid choice".

I read and re-read the instructions, and also re-read the Overthrow rule several times over (on Cole’s embedded recommendation), and I still missed the caveat that the rule only applies to politically suited cards! Somehow I just mentally was thinking that my whole court is “political” and not thinking about the specific suits when I read it before… and now I notice that there is even the purple crown symbol for that suit right next to the rule! 🤦‍♂️

I didn’t get it until reading up on these forums (for exactly these kinds of details), and seeing people pointing out that tribes are only placed by politically-suited cards, and then seeing some of the player aids that emphasized the relation to the overthrow rule!

I’m sure everyone else got this from the get-go, but posting here just in case it helps the next newbie that might come along… (I love this community!)

This is definitely the most-missed rule, even with the rulebook's attempt to draw special attention to it. For the same reason you called out -- without thinking specifically about the word "political" in that sentence, it's possible to miss that it's such an important word!
I think this is partially because since PP is a political game by its nature, the name “political” can be a bit too generic and you can think every card is political. Hence the confusion.

I made the same mistake at first, as I think many people probably did.  If they had simply capitalised the word to "Political" I think that would have helped to distinguish it as a specific type of card.  Also I think it would have helped if they had explicitly stated the link between Political cards and tribes, i.e. all Political cards (and only Political cards) allow you to place tribes.  Then the Overthrow rule becomes much more intuitive.  As it is, you have to infer the link from playing.

I totally agree: “Political” would have helped. 

I had not yet realized that all political cards let you place a tribe! That does make the link more intuitive. 😃

My goodness! Thank-you good sir! I've probably played this game 5-6 times over the past few years, and have always taught that the Overthrow rule throws out ALL cards. Which has led to a lot of grumpy looks from my friends. I just happened to be perusing the forums in anticipation of teaching this game tomorrow and saw your post — thank-you good sir!

I would add the purple political symbol on the player aid in the section about the overthrow rule, as I also just spotted that. The second rule I tend to forget is to put the money for the build action on the cards and not in the bank!

Intro to these “overviews before rules” I do:
The goal is to make reading rules easier, for those who want to spend the time. Sounds weird? I'll try to explain...
I love a variety of games but I find there’s an issue with rulebooks. A catch 22 if you will.
Rulebooks (and rule teaches) must be exact, but that creates a lot of time a feeling of anxiety for people as they start reading and wondering “When will it all tie together for me?”, “when will I say ‘ok, THAT’S the game!’?”. Some rulebooks aren’t read or understood because of that, and it’s a shame as many times the game is simpler than was considered.
To prevent that anxiety you need an overview which tells the story of the game (be it in written or video format). The story needs to be at least as full as to at least be able to quickly say for the majority of elements how they connect to the rest of the game. You tell a story differently than the way someone explains exact rules. The problem is that rulebooks cannot contain such a
Applaud the effort, and so its an irony that that wall of text is more difficult to internalise than the rules.

Much of this script could be very useful; however I find that players take in the rules far better if the basics are explained and we then take one or two learning turns. Have the game set up as if it's in the middle of a game, with some tribes, blocks, spies etc, and use the cards that would be set aside to give each player a small court. Make sure all the action icons are represented. Then each player takes a turn without worrying about tactical implications; they "learn by doing" how to buy from the market, play to their court, use the various action icons, change allegiance etc. Encourage players to use the full range of possibilities (eg if no-one has betrayed, ask someone to betray and take a prize; if no-one has changed suit, demonstrate that).

I find it far more effective than just expecting players to passively take it all in. The only stumbling block is having no dominance check cards if you've already prepared the deck; I've been meaning to scan and print a couple of proxie

Applaud the effort, and so its an irony that that wall of text is more difficult to internalise than the rules.
That's an empirical question that can only be answered by people who didn't understand the rules up until now, or didn't read the rules up until now... not for someone who knows the rules, nor me.
However, had I had the resources, it would be better served as a video. I agree.

I also applaud the effort. As a personal 'script' and the order of key elements/concepts to talk through, I'm sure it's served you well. 

If I'm nitpicking it really needs a proper edit and proofread by other experienced players. There are some oddities and things that may serve to confuse not clarify. 

Examples include, describing 11 cylinders per player (there are only 10. There's a similar shaped score track marker). Or using "allegiance" when the rules use "loyalty". Why not just use the actual term rather than introduce a new concept of allegiance, that I don't think appears in the rules? Or then describing allegiance to "armies" when it's clearer as loyalty to a coalition. And so on. 

As a suggestion, as your intention is to tell the story of the game, you might include early on that the players are each Afghan leaders seeking to win control (VP). 

But, I applaud the effort.

From another thread:
I think the rerolling rules are the most misunderstood rules in the game. It would help if there was a separate thread detailing exactly what happens in various situations. There is a dual face on the dice that causes confusion regarding if you an roll it again and other things like 'if available' on cards that really could do with a detailed thread explaining officially what exactly is allowed and what isn't.


FOOD AND REROLLS

- The key rule:

"If the birdfeeder tray is ever empty, throw all 5 dice back in.
If the dice in the tray all show the same face (including if there is only 1 die) and you are about to gain food for any reason, you may first throw all 5 dice back into the birdfeeder. ( counts as its own unique face.)"

- Let's say you place your action cube in the fourth column of the forest habitat (which shows 2 food dice and an optional card->food dice conversion). You must take 1 die from the birdfeeder (you may reroll before if one dice face is showin

A question that always gets asked when I teach this game relates to the cards "have the fewest". I am of the understanding that zero is less than any but in their defense card says score points for birds in area with the least. I think the official ruling was zero is the least but am looking for confirmation.

Thanks for this. 0 is indeed the fewest - I'll add it.
The only thing I've found in the rules that needs clarification is whether the marginal area's are "slots". Everything else is already in there.
Thanks for this! A few of these were very helpful.

- If a power includes "... bird...", it refers to birds which have been played into that specific habitat, not every bird that could live in that habitat. For example, if a power reads: "Player(s) with the fewest  birds: draw 1 ", only count birds that have been played into the wetland habitat.
The wording of this could be misconstrued, as there are some birds (at least one) that can move from one habitat zone to another after being played. Instead of “have been played into”, perhaps “are currently in” would be more precise.

I'd like to receive a clarification because Italian rules are a bit ambiguous.
When in the birdfeeder there are two dice showing let's say a seed and the face with 2 symbols (invertebrate and seed), can you reroll before taking food? Afet readind the English rules I guess that you cannot do that, but the Italian version leaves space for doubts and we had a discussion about this rule in our playing group.

2) there are 2x of one type of food and 1x of another type.
3) I'll take one of another type and in the birdfeeder remain just 2 dice with the same type of food - can I, in the middle of the turn, reroll all of the dice because of the same symbol on remaining 2 dice?
4) reroll
5) finishing the action = taking remaining 2 dice

I suppose this situation is not possible, please confirm:

1) I can take 3 dice with food through the action
2) there are 2x of one type of food and 1x of another type.
3) I'll take one of another type and in the birdfeeder remain just 2 dice with the same type of food - can I, in the middle of the turn, reroll all of the dice because of the same symbol on remaining 2 dice?
4) reroll
5) finishing the action = taking remaining 2 dice

I suppose this situation is not possible, please confirm:You check for the optional reroll before you take each die. So you can take one die then reroll if the remaining dice are the same, even in the middle of a turn.

REPEATING POWERS

- With four birds in a habitat, A, B, C and D, where C is the bird with a power that reads: "Repeat a brown power on one other bird in this habitat", you could choose to activate ANY bird's brown power in the row as part of C.

If you chose to repeat A's power, you activate D, then A (instead of C), then B, then A.




I find the semantics of the term 'repeat' is a bit misleading. In your example we were debating on whether only D would count as 'repeating' since the other birds have not been activated yet (hence it is not a 'repeat').

2985275.body:
We've just made a big update to the Wingspan rulepop. Check it out!

https://rulepop.com/wingspan

New Content

After this update, the site combines:

* Wingspan Rulebook
* Wingspan Appendix
* Wingspan Automa Rulebook
* Wingspan Asia Rulebook
* Wingspan Asia Appendix
* Wingspan Asia Automated
* European Expansion Rulebook (with appendix and Automa rules)
* Oceania Expansion Rulebook (with appendix)
* Oceania Expansion Automa Rulebook

Whew!

Dynamic Rules Logic

By our count there are now 324 ways to play Wingspan! Each one of those ways combines the rules differently. It can be a daunting task to keep track of which rules apply, and presenting all of the rules at once would be overwhelming.

So, we've integrated logic and settings that change the scope and content of the rules presented. Just click the settings icon in the upper-right of the Wingspan rulepop.

For example, if you set your opponent to “Automa”, the Automa rules appear in the main navigation, and all of the Quick Refere

Wow, awesome. 

Question: is the default set-up for base Wingspan and all the expansions? When I click on "Standard Mode" it appears to make me choose between using base Wingspan or Wingspan Asia. Furthermore, it asks me to select only European and Oceania expansions. 

In short, how do I set up the rule pop for Wingspan plus all 3 expansions, using Oceania nectar boards (and NOT using duet or flock modes)?

Like so:


Asia is both a stand-alone game and and expansion, so I guess that selecting both base and Asia in the first section tells Rulepop to include those rules.

Btw, the base game now also is just as much an expansion for Asia as the other way around! Maybe it helps if you look at it that way. And big respect to Elizabeth Hargrave for designing it that way.

And it's a good thing that you mention the nectar boards option. Playing with Nectar is the default when playing with Oceania, but you can leave out all nectar-related content (food, birds, boards, etc.). Is that an official way to play that Rulepop should support?

Erik's correct on all points here.

The Wingspan rulepop logic assumes that you're using nectar when you include the Oceania expansion. Including yet another logic trigger to separate the two makes my brain hurt. 🤯

And yes. The initial settings are for a standard game with all expansions. There's also a little indicator for your current settings just below the main navigation.
Erik's always right, right?  He's the owl after all.

Hey everybody, I'm the rules editor and usability developer for Oath. I'm excited to say that the Oath PNP is now released, and I'm posting this thread to collate any answers to rules questions that may come up.

The public PNP is here.

Here are some ground rules to make everyone's time easier.

#1: No New Threads. Please do not post new threads with rules questions for this PNP. We are creating this thread to minimize the number of outdated answers to rules present in future BGG searches when Oath is released. (We had a few problems upon the release of Root where people were referencing old PNP rules threads.)

#2: Questions Only. For ease of browsing this thread, please keep your posts to questions, not suggestions or comments or answers to other people's questions. If you have any suggestions or comments, please send them to editor (at) joshuayearsley (dot) com or post them as Dropbox comments on the rulebook.

#3: This Release Is Not Final. This release is still in heavy developme

Seeing that the price of the game + shipping to my country is so high, it's going to be hard to get this game. Is there a plan to release a full final PNP?

Edit: not free PNP, paid PNP I can buy.

Seeing that the price of the game + shipping to my country is so high, it's going to be hard to get this game. Is there a plan to release a full final PNP?

I would be so annoyed at questions like this if I were a game developer. To me, this reads as, “I don’t want to pay the price you’re asking, so I demand that you provide me a full copy of the game for free.”

A PnP should be used to try a game out, not to replace it. This is Leder Games’ job. They need to sell their game to eat. If it’s too expensive for you, then fair enough. But I don’t think they owe anybody a free, printable copy of the game they’ve put so much effort into. 

(Note that this will be available at retail. If you’re this interested, you could look into whether a local retailer will be able to stock it for a lower price. They can sometimes lean on distribution channels that make distribution a lot cheaper than a small games company like Leder can negotiate for).
Currently we do not have a plan to release a final PNP. It's not completely out of the question, but it's unlikely.

All questions about components, printing instructions, etc. will be answered on the cover sheet of the PNP kit when it's posted. Never fear!

2628630.body:
Hi there! I'm Josh, editor and developer at Leder Games. I'm happy to see so many people enjoying Oath. This thread will collect all the important resources related to Oath, along with some answers to frequently asked questions.

Please do not post new rules questions to this thread. Only post questions related to FAQ and errata entries. This will help people searching through the forums to find the correct thread, and it will help people looking through this thread.

Important Resources
You can find the latest printed Law, Playbook, and player aids here — scroll down to Resources
You can find the live errata and clarifications document here
You can find the Oath card database and FAQ here — warning: card spoilers!
You can find the order of the card packets here — use this if you want to use the card-based first-game setup or walkthrough again

Frequently Asked Questions
You'll find answers to detailed rules questions in the Card Database and the Errata and Clarifications doc above.

I

I don't understand the 5.4.1 errata which removes "or if they have no faceup advisers" from this clarification sentence: "You cannot recover the Darkest Secret from another player if their site has no cards or if they have no faceup advisers."
Looking at the general rule ("You can only recover the Darkest Secret if any card at the holder’s site does not match any of their advisers, or if you are recovering it from yourself."), it seems true that you cannot ever recover the Darkest Secret if it is held by another player and if that player has no faceup advisers.

I don't understand the 5.4.1 errata which removes "or if they have no faceup advisers" from this clarification sentence: "You cannot recover the Darkest Secret from another player if their site has no cards or if they have no faceup advisers."
Looking at the general rule ("You can only recover the Darkest Secret if any card at the holder’s site does not match any of their advisers, or if you are recovering it from yourself."), it seems true that you cannot ever recover the Darkest Secret if it is held by another player and if that player has no faceup advisers.


The errata means that if a player has no face-up advisors you can always recover the Darkest Secret from them, assuming their site has cards. The original rule was causing confusion because people have different interpretations of the word "any." (if Card A doesn't match Card B because Card B doesn't exist, does that count as a mismatch or not?) This change was made because it ultimately simplifies the number of exceptions you

Well if the general rule is not clear, then the general rule should be changed, not an "optional" clarification. Why not add something to the general rule: "You can only recover the Darkest Secret if holder does not have any adviser, if any card at the holder’s site does not match any of their advisers, or if you are recovering it from yourself.

There have been so many efforts to re-phrase that rule...

"You can protect the DS against recovery from other players by having advisers. If there are any cards at your site, all of your advisers must also match at least one of them."

Couldn't help but try it again myself, pretty sure it's not optimal yet (is it even correct, help me folks...?). Probably Leder team will lock themselves in for an entire day and triumphantly come up with the final version of this at some point... and probably we shouldn't be hijacking this thread any longer...

Joshua, I am just wondering where the non card FAQ is? I realise that it represents only a small proportion compared with the card FAQ but the errata and clarifications you refer to here is virtually identical to the October one.

I've updated the Darkest Secret clarification to give fuller guidance. That said, I don't think there's a need to update the core text at this time. The reason I changed the clarification is that ultimately there is a much stronger case for interpreting the core text as meaning what the clarification now states. (That is, if a card has nothing to match to, then the card does not match anything.)

Joshua, I am just wondering where the non card FAQ is? I realise that it represents only a small proportion compared with the card FAQ but the errata and clarifications you refer to here is virtually identical to the October one.

You're looking at it. Currently it just has clarifications and errata directly related to text issues, but I will update it if I start seeing lots of the same question pop up in these forums. The "Weird Things About Oath" page on the back of the playbook is basically just an FAQ, as well.

Thanks. Is there a thematic explanation for the banner of secrets recovery rule that could help players memorize these details? I guess it’s something to do with a traitor at the site who's not being watched by / loyal to court overlords?

Also many thanks to people in the community who've been doing a great job getting to questions and answering them correctly before I even see them. It's helped me focus on updating the Oath card FAQ database and other resources!

In the future, questions like this that are unrelated to the specifics of the resources, errata, and clarifications here should be left to other threads, so that the answers are easier

The Clockwork Prince has a token I don't understand. It's a white token with what looks like a sword and shield icon on it.

The Clockwork Prince's mind states that if the threat is Vision of Faith, and you can't play a card, you should gain one Warband, one Secret, and this symbol.

I can't find any other reference to the symbol anywhere in the rules. What does it do?

It's the symbol for the Prince's Tactics. There's a tracker for it on their board. During certain cases, such as when the Prince draws battle plans, you move it to the right by one. It gives the Prince an extra combat advantage.

2634322.body:
I've been reading a lot of posts here recently and since I've seen this in a lot of them, figured it could be good to set a kind of reminder here in the forum about the walkthrough.

A lot of people seem to be just reading through the game's walkthrough, but the thing about a walkthrough is that you're actually supposed to walk through it. Set up the board with your group and do it step by step. It really helps grasp WHY you're doing things, which is awesome for a first play. Just reading it is fine, but you'll miss the big picture stuff it's supposed to help you... well, through.

That's it :P

I can attest, I read through all the rules a couple times and things didn't click for me until I sat down on Tabletop Simulator and ran through the walkthrough. Only then did the rules and interactions start coming together in my head. The rules seem to have little addendums and exceptions that don't immediately tie into other rules exclusively in the context of the rulebook; the rulebook is best served by being read alongside the card effects to understand why those rules exist and what function they serve. I can understand why it was rough to adjust any cards in the game.

I was one of those people who posted recently and I can attest that setting up the game yesterday and seeing the guided first turn play out really helped me to understand the rules. I was reading it, but it wasn’t making sense, but seeing it play out was what really helped me. 

Fernando speaks the truth. If you want to learn this game most effectively, setting it up, even if it’s just for you to learn, really helps. There is also a file in the Files section that show you how to reset you decks back to the way they were when you first opened them. I did that yesterday really for my first proper game with friends.

2729259.body:
Last night we played our second game, and the chancellor rolled a 6 again with the purple die at the end of the fifth round.. Pretty frustrating when our first game had the exact same scenario. Chances of this happening twice in a row are, you guessed it, 1/36. Pretty anti-climactic.

At this point an exile was the usurper and another exile completed his vision of sanctuary with 4 relics. So basically, chances were slim the chancellor would have won. We packed it all up and the chancellor built the festival district edifice.

Only later we realized that the chancellor isn't allowed to throw the die when he is NOT the oathkeeper, and ofcourse, now this rule clicks. This makes the purple die mechanism more balanced and it guarantees a struggle for the oathkeeper title - making a win this way less anti-climactic and more deserved. 

Anyway, we made up that the chancellor committed fraud, got away with it, and built a festival district to cloud the minds of the masses. But we will NEVAH fo
Just fyi there's still a roll if a citizen is Oathkeeper. You only skip the roll if an exile is holding the title.

This is such a crucial rule. I was so disappointed when Quackalope completely misunderstood it in their gameplay / final thoughts, as it was their #1 criticism of the game; believing Oath could always inevitably end on the 5th round on a dice roll of 6, or lower rolls in following rounds.

Really do hope they take the chance to play the game without so many mistakes, as they make it clear they think Cole didn't know how to end a game of Oath and that the mechanic isn't well thought out. It's actually quite a thoughtful and nuanced mechanic, especially considering the Chancellor takes the first turn each round and can't actively react to Exiles trying to take the Oathkeeper title (in turn making Citizenship an incredibly powerful defensive tool, which is then balanced by the availability of Successorship). 

Although cards can grant incredible, sweeping powers, Oath's core gameplay mechanics become more delicately balanced the better you understand them.

That review really convinced me they are way too surface level to be taken seriously. They seem to be more focused on traveling the country every week and pumping out 15 videos a week than getting a handle on the rules of a game before they review it.

People call Oath random, and it's true you roll lots of dice at crucial moments and the card draws are extreme. But whenever I look back at a game I played, I can always trace whatever happened to decisions taken. The outcomes have everything to do with the way people choose to play, the way they position themselves in the unfolding drama. Strangely, for all its swinginess, it never feels random to me.

Wait a second: if I understood correctly before, whenever an exile or a citizen gets to fulfill the Oath, they get the Oathkeeper title. Only on their next wake, if they are an exile, they would flip it to Usurper, which would stop the end game rolls (as it is written on the Usurper title itself). 

Are you saying that the endgame rolls stop as soon as they fulfill the Oath, even before flipping it to the Usurper side?

Are you saying that the endgame rolls stop as soon as they fulfill the Oath, even before flipping it to the Usurper side?

 If it is the end of the fifth, sixth, or seventh round, roll the die if the Chancellor or a Citizen is the Oathkeeper.

Last night I was introduced to Oath. Our game of 4 players, playing first game using the tutorial, took about 4 hours, and only mercifully ended when the Chancellor rolled a 6 at the soonest possible moment. It was a miserable, drawn-out, rules-lawyering nightmare. And yet - I loved the game. It was incredible and unlike anything I had ever played. But what. a. slog.

So, to help other folks out of the box, below is a list of rules questions we encountered in our first game, so you don't have to go searching every time these come up (and how they will come up...)

Banners

The People's Favor
The people's favor is kept by either adding a favor token from your supply, or if you cannot, removing one and adding it to a bank. But, says the rules, the People's Favor cannot lose its last token. So what then do you do if you have no favor in your inventory, and only one token is left on the Banner? The answer is - nothing. You neither add nor remove, and you are more vulnerable to having it ta

Thank you! That was hard to find an answer for. I'll update above.

We lost a LOT of time to these questions, and it made for an exhausting session that could have easily ruined the game altogether. I plan to give it another go for sure, but best of luck to all who try and invest in that first session.

One recommended way of learning the game is to make snap rulings and check afterwards what the actual rule is. It means you have to accept that sometimes people enjoy an advantage “illegally”, but usually the effect on game balance is much less than that of the game’s powers themselves. Having that tempo does help in enjoying and also in learning the game. And it’s OK to accept that it will take a lot of games before you’re easy enough with everything and getting every ruling right. (Even 100 games in some powers and unforeseen effects keep surprising me!)

Some of the issues here can be resolved if you follow the steps listed in the Law (for the search and for the campaign action) very literally. E.g. battle plans are announced before effects are applied so indeed, the Sticky Fire could not have been used by the winner.

The 3 value green die is right. The value is dependent on your workers in the mill (plus bonus); it does not matter what value was on the blue die.

2562742.body:
Looks to me like the investment track is really of length two as the first and third spaces are irrelevant. There is never a reason to advance only a single space when taking an investment action.

Going to space 1 or 3 gives no immediate benefit and, given the rules which always permit you to advance 1 or 2 spaces on a track, going to 1 or 3 doesn't get you any closer to a position which does provide such a benefit. I see no tempo games available where it is useful to move your 2 spaces over 2 different turns as going slowly doesn't permit you to, for instance, defer passing and dropping out as passing does not mean you drop out of this phase. If you have only the $1 left to do a single space advance, you still have that same $1 next round as there is no taxes or expenses phase.

Am I missing something?

No, you seem to understand it ok. It is a rare situation when you may only want to spend $1. You would generally pay the $2 and advance to the next space that gives you a benefit. The option is there for you if you want it to only spend the $1.

Hi all:

Looking through the starter cards again, I think the top action of Boldening Blow, due to the formatting, will be misread by more than a few people, so I wanted to make a post to clarify.

The attack shows a pattern attack with Banner Spear and two allies and then a bunch of red hexes. The card says Attack 4, and then in a bubble "target one enemy in the red hexes, disarm"

(Then you bless your allies who helped you make the pattern. Cool!)

This is commonly mistaken as "I get to attack all these hexes for 4, and then pick one enemy to disarm". However it's just an Attack 4 disarm on one enemy, with the additional bless effect.  This is the only Banner Spear formation attack to target one enemy but show multiple hexes, so it's an easy point of confusion. 

As Banner Spear is a common starter and I 100% know it will lead to more than one question on here, I thought I'd mention that one early! 

You can see the card at this link, but know that it shows Banner Spear cards from le

3014958.body: In this situation, the monster (M) has Movement 1, Range 2, Target 2 and is hemmed in by obstacles (in brown). According to Gloomhaven and JOTR rules, it would prioritize losing disadvantage on its focus (C1) and move to a, at the expense of losing its second target (C2). However, in Frosthaven, monsters seek to maximize targets before minimizing disadvantage, so it would stay put. Is this correct?
Makes sense - 1 target at advantage and 1 at disadvantage is clearly better than just 1 target at advantage

EDIT:  This is incorrect.  See below.

My reading of the FH rules is that the only time monsters try to lose disadvantage is in multi-target attacks.  if a monster is adjacent to its one-and-only target for a ranged attack, it will not move away to lose disadvantage, correct?  (This is different than the way it was in Gloomhaven.)

See page 42, Monster Movement where it does not instruct use to "minimize disadvantage" except in the section discussing multi-target attacks.

Not correct. The change is rather that in Gloomhaven, monsters lose or avoid Disadvantage on primary focus in preference to attacking additional targets, while in FH attacking additional targets is preferred.
 When a monster performs a ranged attack on an adjacent target, it first moves away from that target if possible, so that the attack does not have disadvantage. When a monster performs ranged attacks on multiple targets, it moves to attack the most possible targets (including its focus), with the fewest possible disadvantaged attacks, while using the fewest possible movement points.
(Emphasis added.)

~J

The focus is the enemy it can perform its attack on using the fewest movement points.  In the example above, the monster can attack either C1 or C2 using 0 movement points, so that condition is a tie.

No (see rulebook)

Yes, they will act directly before your turn on initiative 99 (source)

3235308.body:
I am not sure if these will create much discussion, but I wanted to get ahead of it if so and keep said discussion out of the FAQ thread. Here are the two newer rulings, reposted from the FAQ thread.

(1) Red hex AoE targeting was declared as mandatory in the GH FAQ. Due to some vagueness in the FH rulebook, and to bring it in line with all the other targeting in the game, this ruling is overturned - at least for Frosthaven and forward. Red hex AoE targeting is only mandatory if there's a mandatory box.

(2) Formalization of "end of turn wrap-up."  GH and FH describe a wide variety of things as "end of turn." This has caused some confusion over the timing of effects like Geminate's Harvest the Essence ("at the end of each of your turns, you may consume any element to create ice or light") and certain items that let you do things at the end of your turn. Previous GH and FH FAQ entries have moved towards clarifying a difference between "end of player turn" and "end of turn wrap-up" and t

Addendum - 

2024-01-27 Backlog Clearing Part 3 - Prior Ruling Overturning Edition

This applies to multiple FAQ entries that I will be editing individually today. The edits aren't done yet - I only have time for this note right now - but they are in progress. Please don't post about "missed edits" until tomorrow, at which point I welcome extra sets of eyes :)

There has been a lot of discussion about - particularly - placing overlays adjacent to enemies after that enemy had died. A previous ruling was that, because the target died, there is no longer a "reference" for the placement of the new overlay, and thus it basically errors out and doesn't actually place the overlay.

This prior ruling (a) wasn't particularly fun and was probably misplayed all the time, and (b) was inconsistent with some previous rulings in GH1e, particularly around Cragheart's Massive Boulder. There's also a simple framework for it which we missed before, and will be correcting now. (Special thanks to gripeaway

I think the "reference dead enemy" ruling only prevents the drifter level 9 card from firing off on a kill, at least among Frosthaven classes. I can't think of any other cards where you could try to reference a dead enemy's position on a seperate ability that doesn't have wording or an exception that makes it work anyway.

Well, this is my assuming the ruling is applicable to non-overlay effects and abilities that reference an enemy's position.

At face value, this would stop "chain attack" type abilities, like Hatchet's ricochet, if the original target dies. Or rather, perhaps it was always like that, but people took it for granted and didn't really think about it.

Don't take this as relevant to JotL at this time. I'm only doing the Frosthaven FAQ. 🙂

Edit - and yes, a lot of effort has been made to "word around" this in the past. Some of that may be redundant.

About the end of turn effects. Where does short resting fall into this? 
I can imagine there can still be timing issues involving damage taken and the position of cards.

My gut feeling says short resting should be another stage in between end of turn effects and the wrap-up.


For the other entries, I fully agree. The AoE one is a bit unexpected, but it could work either way.


Edit:
I'm nothing the Prism dotted line as an erratum on my copy.
Short resting is a separate end of round step, not end of turn. By then it probably shouldn't matter?

What about an attack with curse?  Previously if the enemy died the curse would not get entered into the enemy attack deck. I'm guessing this differs to the overlay because the curse needs the enemy, rather than the hex itself.

(Also what's AMD stand for?)

The curse still won't happen, nor will any other negative conditions or forced movement.

You do still need an enemy for those. (Edit - page 28 is clear, here, for the rule.)

AMD = Attack Modifier Deck.

All of this being said, to get back to my related question from the initial thread… under this new ruling, if I play Lava bomb and draw a Push 2 AMD, and the enemy survives, does the lava get created on the enemy’s initial hex, or in the push’s destination hex? Or ambiguous?

All of this being said, to get back to my related question from the initial thread… under this new ruling, if I play Lava bomb and draw a Push 2 AMD, and the enemy survives, does the lava get created on the enemy’s initial hex, or in the push’s destination hex? Or ambiguous?
I'd argue ambiguous, like other times when you get both push and create an overlay.

Short resting is a separate end of round step, not end of turn. By then it probably shouldn't matter?

2512694.body: can someone pls explain why the salmon score in the attached game-end layout on the web version of the solo mode below is 8 please? thanks

The salmon between the bear and eagle and the salmon between the eagle and fox are touching 3 or more other salmon tiles. Those 2 salmon tiles are disqualified from the salmon scoring, so you have a run of 2 salmon tokens at the bottom and then 2 single salmon tokens (top most and left most salmon tokens) left. 4+2+2=8pts.

The salmon between the bear and eagle and the salmon between the eagle and fox are touching 3 or more other salmon tiles. Those 2 salmon tiles are disqualified from the salmon scoring, so you have a run of 2 salmon tokens at the bottom and then 2 single salmon tokens (top most and left most salmon tokens) left. 4+2+2=8pts.
I'm gonna need some big X markers to remove these bad salmon from my runs with checking the scores.

When scoring a salmon run, the rulebook states:

Each run of salmon may not have any other salmon adjacent to it.

I read this as similar to the bear requirements - that if there's another salmon adjacent to the run, the whole run does not count.  However, it seems that the web version just ignores the "disqualifying" salmon and just doesn't consider them part of a run.

How should this be played?

As Gavin noted, David has it correct. Think of it this way - every salmon that violates that rule doesn't count toward any run. So, you could virtually flip them over then score the salmon. The game in question has 2 salmon that violate that rule and if you remove them you end up with runs of 2, 1, & 1 which gives you 4+2+2 = 8 points.

The important takeaway is that this something you should avoid at all costs. Better to discard the salmon that would trigger the rule violation. I don't believe the online demo allows you to do that though.

If you're allowed to just ignore the problematic salmon, what's stopping you from ignoring a problematic bear?  Neither rule allows for an extra adjacent animal and removing animals is not something listed in the rulebook.  If I were to be scoring the above situation without seeing this thread, I'd assume the entire salmon run would be 0 points.  

So the follow-up to this is can you ignore problematic bears?  Can you have a group larger than what w

Thanks for the question, Joshua. The bear scoring is very specific about groups needing not be away from other bears as it is the definition of bear scoring across all cards. Salmon runs are a little more interesting, and this distinction can be more impactful. So, this lets the player salvage some points from what is otherwise a malformed run.

I guess I just don't understand why a "malformed" run is any different than a "malformed" group of bears.  I don't mind the kinder scoring, I just assumed otherwise based on the language on the cards.

I understand a salmon added to a triangle run is invalid. But what if during scoring this situation is discovered and the player does not know which came first, the run or the triangle? Would he have to take the scoring as described (8 points) or could he ignore the one triangle salmon, leaving the 5 salmon run and score the 15 points?

Would he have to take the scoring as described (8 points) or could he ignore the one triangle salmon, leaving the 5 salmon run and score the 15 points? 
You would have to ignore any salmon that are touching more than 2 other salmon. This could result in creating 2 separate runs.

I'm really glad I found this thread. In the rulebook it says 'Each run of salmon may not have any other
salmon adjacent to it', but there is no mentioning of what happens when this rule is violated. The same goes for the bears and the hawks. At first I thought I wasn't allowed to even place a salmon adjacent to an already existing run. Then I thought the whole run wouldn't score if I was forced to place it adjacent. Now it seems you filter out the tokens that violate the rule. Something to add to the rulebook when you consider a reprint! ;)

2701568.body:
Please help me!

The text of the Hawk Scoring Card B says the following:

Scores for each HAWK that is not adjacent to any other HAWK and has a direct line of sight to a HAWK.

A general rule for the HAWK scoring cards says:

A line of sight is a STRAIGHT LINE for FLAT SIDE to FLAT SIDE of hexagons.

I am extremely confused how to score certain hawks with this card!

Attatched you find pictures of player 2 and player 3.

When it comes to scoring, how many points do player 2 + 3 get when you see the constellation on each picture?

Player 2:


Player 3:

Hi there!
Player 2 would score 12 points, because they have 4 hawks that each have a line of sight to at least one other hawk.
Player 3 would score 9 points, because they have 3 hawks that each have a line of sight to at least one other hawk.
Hope that helps! :)

That helps a lot!
Thank you so much, Shawn!

I would've said 10 points (2 sets of 2) for Player 2 - I'm guessing that was your interpretation too?

I haven't read the rulebook, but based on the wording of the definition and the diagram on the card that makes the most sense to me.
It says for each hawk not each pair of hawks.

It says for each hawk not each pair of hawks.

That's correct, Joe, but what I intuit from the definition of Line of Sight is that each hex has 6 lines of sight - one from each flat side - so Hawk Top Left cannot see Hawk Top Right.

I mentioned 2 sets of 2 Hawks for the sake of clarity - scoring 2 Hawks twice rather than 4 Hawks once.

Right, but you count each hawk that meets the conditions. Then you get points according to that number of hawks. If you have 4 hawks that are not adjacent to a hawk and have another hawk in line of sight then you get 12 points. The fact that they are paired off is irrelevant.

The iconography on that card seems really confusing. Cause it says only hawks that are not adjacent to another Hawk score and yet the hawks that are used to demonstrate scoring on that card are completely surrounded by hawks. It makes no sense to me.
Those hawks have Xs through them. This is  standard iconography on these cards to show that the animal can't be in that space for scoring. See the Salmon and Bear A cards for the same type of symbol.

You are amazing!!! 😍

2730496.body:
One little bit that wasn't clear to me in a game we played yesterday. A player wiped all of the wildlife tokens with a nature token. The 4 new tokens came up, and it was a three of a kind. Can that player then choose to wipe those three tokens for free?

It was unclear to me because the order of reading the rules seem to indicate that wiping for three/four of a kind happens at the start of the turn, and playing nature tokens happens during the turn.
We've played so that at any point, when you have three of the same tokens, you can swap them out.

Hi Mike, thanks for the question. Overpopulation can happen at any point during your turn before you make your choice of tile & token. For wiping three of a kind, the restriction is just that you can only do it once per turn.

So, nature tokens can lead to all sorts of combinations in this area. You could choose to wipe some with a nature token then 4 of the same could come up which would force a full wipe. After that you might use a second nature token to wipe some then 3 of the same could come up which would allow you to choose to wipe those 3.

Maybe the "alternative rules for faster play" from the landmarks expansion are meant here?
https://boardgamegeek.com/filepage/278833/cascadia-landmarks-english-rulebook

Yes, it has to be that.

The Landmarks expansion adds support for five and six players, so it also adds that optional rule to make the game faster. Instead of 20 rounds in a game, where each player drafts a total of 20 landscape tiles paired with 20 wildlife tokens, the game now lasts 15 rounds instead. Each player starts the game with a personal set of five landscape/wildlife pairs in front of them that can be used between turns.

While the rule is meant for larger player count games, it can be used at any player count. Jens' link above takes you to the expansion rules from the expansion's bgg page.

Cheers!
This is what I was referring too. It makes the game much better in my opinion because you can plan for sets of animals/tiles you definitely have.

Can you apply those "alternative rules for faster play" if you only own the base game?
Or do you need to own the expansion and mix the expansion tiles into the game before then applying the tile removals described in the  "alternative rules for faster play"?

Can you apply those "alternative rules for faster play" if you only own the base game?
Or do you need to own the expansion and mix the expansion tiles into the game before then applying the tile removals described in the  "alternative rules for faster play"?

It absolutely works fine with just the base game. To use the Faster Play rule, you will just setup the game as you normally would. After getting the proper amount of Landscape Tiles you will use in your game (based on Player count), you will then pull five tiles per player out of those tiles, and deal them out to each player, and then randomly assign a Wildlife token to each tile. Then start the game normally, but with each player having a private stock of five Landscape Tiles + Wildlife Tokens they can use between their turns.

For example, in a 3-player game you will setup a stack of 63 Landscape Tiles to use for your game (by removing 22 tiles). Then from those 63 tiles you will deal five tiles to each player as their private s

To use the Faster Play rule, you will just setup the game as you normally would. After getting the proper amount of Landscape Tiles you will use in your game (based on Player count), you will then pull five tiles per player out of those tiles, and deal them out to each player, and then randomly assign a Wildlife token to each tile. Then start the game normally, but with each player having a private stock of five Landscape Tiles + Wildlife Tokens they can use between their turns.

For example, in a 3-player game you will setup a stack of 63 Landscape Tiles to use for your game (by removing 22 tiles). Then from those 63 tiles you will deal five tiles to each player as their private stock. Then each player will pull five Wildlife Tokens from the bag and randomly assign one token to each tile. Then you are all set up.
I'm confused how this set up speeds the game. What do you mean when you say that players can use their private stock between their turns?

Here are the Landmarks rules again if anyone wants to read them: PDF. The Faster Play variant is on page 4.

Yes, you can play it with the base game. It was added to the expansion because it's especially useful in higher player counts, not supported by the base game.

Players have 5 chances to play from their private stock while other players take their turn. Players get fewer "regular" turns. So the total turn count is smaller, making the game shorter.

Quoting from the end:
In this “faster play” setup, each player will only play a total of 15 main turns, rather than 20, and they will play a total of 5 additional between-turn actions between their turns. This means that by the end of the game, players will have added 20 Habitat Tiles and 20 Wildlife Tokens to their environment (the same number as the standard rules). The added action between turns will reduce the overall playtime and works especially well when playing with 5 or 6 players.

I'm confused how this set up speeds the game. What do you mean when you say that players can use their private stock between their turns?

You play from your private stock simultaneously while *other* players are taking their turn (between your normal turns, as I said above). With 15 turns instead of 20, coupled with playing 5 tiles during other players turns, the game should last 3/4 the amount of time a normal game takes.

Cheers!

I find the official background story in the rule book a bit lacking in its connection with the actual game mechanics. Take for example the premise that you are on a newly discovered island that has no inhabitants. How then can you trade anything for your gold coins?
I think it much more logical if you have at least established some resemblance of a city on the coast of the island.

Anyway, here is my take on a bit different background story. I hope some of you may like it.

================================


Introduction to Arnak


Welcome to Arnak, and also let me be one of the first to congratulate you of becoming a member of our Archaeologists Guild.
My name is Arnold and I am the head of our excellent research museum. I know you are new here, so please let me explain to you a bit how things works around here on this remote island. We have dominantly two kinds of people that we care about. There are the members of our Archaeologist Guild, and then there are all those other non-membe

I haven't read the rules yet,  but this should be in there! 

At first the compass-bucks seemed a little weird,  but you made it all make sense,  and I think thematically this might be a good way to start explaining the rules! 
Well done,  it was entertaining.
This needs to be an official job.  A guy who goes back into games and makes the story make sense with the mechanics. Love it.   This is great writing.
Anyone else has a take on how to explain the rules in a story?

2664297.body:
On page 11 of the rules it says how the card row behaves.

It has 4 steps about how to buy an item and how to buy an artifact. In both cases it has as step 4 "Refill the card row".

One should think then that it is settled, and that it is clear, that each time you buy a card, be it an item or an artifact, it is a part of the process (the last step of the act of buying), that is when you refill the card row.

But that is not so. Because under it (on the same page 11) the paragraph with the heading "Refilling the card row" starts with "At the end of your turn, if the card row is missing a card, refill the row with a card of the same type". This says the timing is different, it says "At the end of your turn".



So which is it?

And why does it matter? Well, normally it would not matter much, because you can only take one main action during your turn, and buying a card is a main action. But you have two artifacts that lets you activate assistants on the board, and one assistant has the ef
These two are not exclusive, the card buy action lets you refill. The other rule might be for any other case that has a card removed from the card row.

These two are not exclusive, the card buy action lets you refill. The other rule might be for any other case that has a card removed from the card row.
I want an official ruling on this. Because if you are right, then the BGA implementation is wrong.

And why does it matter? Well, normally it would not matter much, because you can only take one main action during your turn, and buying a card is a main action. But you have two artifacts that lets you activate assistants on the board, and one assistant has the effect that it lets you buy a new card with a discount. So in that case you can buy two cards without your turn ending in between. So will you have one less card to choose from in that case, the second time you buy and it has not yet been the end of your turn?

Buying a card is a single action, the last step of which is refilling the card row. In the case you describe, you are performing two card buy actions, one as a main action, one as a free action. You refill after the first one, and have a full row to select from for your second buy.

Buying a card is a single action, the last step of which is refilling the card row. In the case you describe, you are performing two card buy actions, one as a main action, one as a free action. You refill after the first one, and have a full row to select from for your second buy.

Yes, that is what I thought at first too. Then you are going with the interpretation of the first half of page 11 of the rules. But then you are ignoring the timing of the "refill the row" that is clearly spelled out on the bottom of the page: "At the end of your turn ..."

Thank you for bringing this issue to our attention. We should make it clearer in future reprints.
BGA implementation corresponds with our design intent. You refill the card row when you end your turn.

FWIW I see no reason to think that the bottom of the page text saying to refill at the end of your turn somehow nullifies or contradicts the card purchasing text saying to refill after you purchase.

There's no contradiction between refilling after purchasing a card and also refilling if the row is empty at the end of your turn: the card row can be missing a card for other reasons than a card purchase (which by the card purchase rules would indeed have already refilled the row).

E.g. the artifacts Monkey Medallion (Gain item and place it on the top of your deck) and Ornate Hammer (Exile the rightmost item in the card row...) will evidently leave the card row missing a card.

Edited to add: Heh, I cross-posted with Elwen's comment that the rules mistakenly say to refill after purchasing! :)

There have been several questions about how to resolve ties in combat. The rulebook (page 12) explains the method quite precisely and succinctly. But for players who would like to see examples, I'm creating this post to list all the scenarios that involve ties and how to distribute rewards for them.

For all the following examples, consider the conflict card's rewards to be:
1st: A
2nd: B
3rd: C

3-player Game Examples
Players are: P1, P2, P3

:bd6-1: All 3 players tie for 1st
Each player earns B.

:bd6-2: 2 players (P1, P2) tie for 1st
P1 & P2 each earn B.
P3 earns nothing.

:bd6-3: 2 players (P2, P3) tie for 2nd
P1 earns A.
P2 & P3 each earn C.

4-player Game Examples
Players are: P1, P2, P3, P4

:d10-1: All 4 players tie for 1st
Each player earns B.

:d10-2: 3 players (P1, P2, P3) tie for 1st
P1 & P2 & P3 each earn B.
P4 earns nothing.

:d10-3: 3 players (P2, P3, P4) tie for 2nd
P1 earns A.
P2 & P3 & P4 each earn C.

:d10-4: 2 players (P1, P2) tie for 1st, P3 beats P4 for 3rd
P1 & P

In a four player game the reward count is 3, 1st, 2nd and 3rd. The fourth place combatant gets nothing, correct? In a 4 player game, if two players are tied for third place, they get nothing since there is no 4th place award.
Correct.

So in a three player game, if two players are tied for second why is a third reward now given? Why would they simply not receive a reward?
Because of the rules printed on page 12 of the rulebook:

When players tie for second place, they each receive the third reward.

Players tying for third place receive nothing.

I see that in the rules. My question is why. Again, it doesn’t appear to make sense that in a three player game, when normally there are only two rewards, if there is a tie for second a third reward is given. 

There’s no fourth award given if there’s a tie for third in a 4 player game.

I see that in the rules. My question is why. Again, it doesn’t appear to make sense that in a three player game, when normally there are only two rewards, if there is a tie for second a third reward is given. 

There’s no fourth award given if there’s a tie for third in a 4 player game. 

Yeah, I'm interested to hear reasoning on this as well.  It doesn't make intuitive sense considering the four player rules, which is the main reason there are so many questions here about it.

I see that in the rules. My question is why. Again, it doesn’t appear to make sense that in a three player game, when normally there are only two rewards, if there is a tie for second a third reward is given. 

To achieve desired gameplay.

I don’t think it’s a major bummer to be tied for 3rd in a fourth player game and earn nothing, because the third place prizes are so low. Downgrading a low reward to nothing isn’t a game-breaking blow for those players.

But in a 3-player game, if the winner edges out two other players who happened to be tied, I think it’s significant downgrade in gameplay quality if those two players are downgraded from a medium sized reward to nothing.

Another way to look at this, if you’re looking purely through a consistency lens, is imagine there is a 4th reward printed on each conflict card, and when players are tied for the third, they each receive the 4th reward. Now imagine that reward is “Nothing.”

Having played the game quite a bit with a variety of groups, here's a list of some rules that I've seen overlooked or confused. I wouldn't say all these are very common, but I've seen all of them mistaken or at least asked about, at least once. And some are easy to forget about mid-game. 

If you have played the game once or twice already, I'd recommend looking through these to see if you missed anything:

Overlooked or Mistaken Rules:

 • If you have a Flag token on a board space, and another Conflict card comes up with the name of that location, you get a defensive bonus at the round start: one troop from your Supply directly to the Conflict

• You always pay the cost first when you go to a board location:
1) Pay the cost of the location
2) Perform the benefits of the card and benefits of the space in either order

• The Voice card can only block a board space until that player's next turn that round – not the entirety of the round

• The Baron's ability to move up on the two Influen

Hi everyone, I had seen some people make a request for a comprehensive Dune Rules FAQ, so I spent some time putting one together. Right now, there are a lot of different FAQ and designer rulings spread out over the different rulebooks, BGG threads, Discord posts, etc, and I wanted to created an easily searchable reference tool that links to the original sources. It compiles everything from the Official FAQ, each rulebook's FAQ section, and then various forum posts where Paul Dennen has provided an answer.

- I feel like I'm missing several issues that have come up over the years, so feel free to comment with the note and the official source if you think of an addition
- I highlighted a few areas that to my knowledge have not yet had an official confirmation/ruling. If you have an official source for it please let me know.
- I'll also be keeping an eye on the forums and try to update this doc as any new official rulings come up

I've kept the entries alphabetical in keeping with the way

Which rewards in Dune are NOT an atomic effect?
Power Play’s two sentences are separate effects:
“Trash this card.”
“Gain two influence instead of one.”
What Paul says
"Gain 2 influence instead of 1" is an effect that can be taken at any point in the turn but it is one atomic effect. Your example references "go up 1 more" and that's not an effect on Power Play (or Treachery). emphasis mine. 

Apologies if I am misunderstanding your meaning in relation to the Power Play clarification in your FAQ. 
Again, thank you for taking the time to put it together.

Thanks for the comment! My FAQ may not be clear enough, but it’s trying to say:

- Power Play’s two sentences are NOT combined into an atomic effect. They are two separate effects and may be executed separately. 

- One of those effects, the double bump, is an atomic effect. Nothing can interrupt that double bump.

I'm not sure it's really necessary to define "atomic effects", they're not defined as such in the rules AFAIK? Also, a different name would be better considering that there are now "Family Atomics" (which I thought this was somehow referring to).

I am remined of the monster thread on "Orthogonal" as a gaming term, as we sure did bring in an outside word because it was useful. And of course atomicity is irrelevant to 99% of the game but then super important in some edge cases.

The word "atomic" also means "indivisible", (and may not be related to nuclear atoms from physics). That is the source of the term "atomic actions".

Yeah that whole section is probably TMI for many people, but for those who are really into the rules and edge cases of Dune, I thought it would be helpful to show (and link to) the underlying principles that Dennen has articulated in ruling on various questions. 2762917.body:
We had the following situation: 2-player game (so no State player) - the State had just produced and went into bankrupcy when paying the wages. This triggered an IMF intervention which changed Fiscal Policy from 1B to 1C, so State lost 3 companies.
Before the intervention the storages for Healthcare and Education were full with 12 resources each (limit is 8 potential production +4).
After the intervention the storage capacity is reduced to 8 (limit becomes 4 potential production +4).
What happens to the now surplus resources over 8? Are they lost immediately or is storage limit only checked at time of production?
They are lost immediately. The storage limit is considered to be always in effect - it is not checked at a specific point in the round.

2912386.body:
The London Season is skipped on turn 1, and there is an extra session of retirements at the end of the game (effectively another London Season). 
So structurally (as well in narrative terms) it really feels like the final phase of each turn. Is there a reason why it is depicted as the first phase? This choice has created a couple of exceptions in the rules so it feels like there must be an important point I’m missing.

I know at one point Cole answered this question  with this:

 "... it's largely an aesthetic choices <sic> since the first and last phases of basically any turn structure can usually be juggled back and forth. I think it helps players compose the "budget" for their turn to have it at the start and i like where it sits in the rules setc. <sic>" 

and when asked again, a similar response:

 "There are a bunch of reasons I like to put it at the start. The biggest one is it has primacy when it comes to how the rules are organized and how players budget their turns. but it's largely an gameplay aesthetic choice"

Thanks. It was your video that made me ask the question as it happens. 
In terms of the story arc, London Season feels like the culmination of the turn—you’ve made your loot, now do you get to turn it into points?

Thanks. It was your video that made me ask the question as it happens. 
In terms of the story arc, London Season feels like the culmination of the turn—you’ve made your loot, now do you get to turn it into points?

it does. In terms of rulebook structure, Cole has also explained, it is important players understand the London Season before they get into the rest of the rulebook, so rather than have that section come last, it comes first, so they learn it first, and the rulebook mirrors the turn structure (which is very important in this game, to save on flipping back and forth ), so it goes first, they understand the London Season display and retirements are the objectives in front of you for the turn, and off you go ...

But yes, in my videos I am ending with the start of the next turn's London Season in order to set up the next episode in the video with the "this is how things look for the upcoming turn, join me next time..." type-thing... It does feel like a natural way to do it for
Indeed. If I had a dollar for every time I started learning/teaching boardgames rules by skipping to the end to determine the player's goals...I'd have a lot more boardgames in my collection.

Der Fehler auf dem Spielplan ist ärgerlich, aber auch bei „Größer als Erwartungen in Summe der Dividenden“ hätte ich ein Fragezeichen im Gesicht. 

Bei Violet Effingham muss wahrscheinlich „Werft“ stehen, kann man aber klären, wenn sie in die Auslage gelegt wird.

Insgesamt wirkt es, als wäre die Regel von jemandem übersetzt worden, der das Spiel nie gespielt und die Regel einfach 1:1 übersetzt hat - was teilweise zu merkwürdigen Formulierungen führt. Die englische Regel ist aber auch nicht das gelbe vom Ei. Ohne das Video von Heavy Cardboard, in dem Cole das Spiel erklärt und sie es zu viert spielen, hätte ich einiges nicht verstanden.

Ich bin aber froh, da
